Objects of half a region or more are humongous: they skip the young generation and need contiguous regions. At high allocation rates they fragment the heap until G1 falls back to a Full GC. The half-region threshold is the key number to check.

stages.question: What is the most effective immediate mitigation, and what investigation must accompany it?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the heap to 32 GB. With four times more old-generation space, humongous objects take much longer to fill the heap, so a Full GC should not happen within the busy hour.
options.feedback: Increasing heap extends the interval between Full GCs but does not eliminate them. Eventually, humongous allocation rate will fill even 32GB during sustained peak load. Larger heaps also mean longer Full GC durations when they do occur (more memory to scan). This is a symptom-deferral, not a fix. The 3–6 second Full GC on 8GB could become a much longer pause on a 32GB heap.

options.label: B
options.text: Switch to generational ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational). Its pauses stay below a millisecond, and turn on JFR allocation profiling to find the large allocations.
options.feedback: Reasonable, but not the best first move. Generational ZGC would remove the long pauses, but changing the collector during an incident brings new behaviour (more memory overhead, different tuning) that has not been load-tested. A one-flag change to the region size fixes the trigger with the same, well-known collector; ZGC can then be evaluated properly in a load test.

options.label: C
options.text: Set -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m: the threshold becomes 4 MB, so 2.3 MB buffers are ordinary young objects again. One flag, same collector — plus JFR to find the source.
options.feedback: Correct. With 8 MB regions, only objects of 4 MB or more are humongous, so the 2.3 MB allocations go back to the young generation, where they die young and are collected cheaply. It is a single, low-risk flag on the collector the team already runs. JFR allocation profiling at the same time finds what is allocating the large buffers, because the real fix is to stop allocating them.

options.label: D
options.text: Restart all pods at 07:55 every weekday so each one starts market open with a clean, unfragmented heap, and keep that schedule until the code is fixed.
options.feedback: Scheduled restarts are a last resort for applications with unresolvable memory leaks. They create a brief unavailability window (pod restart + JVM warmup = 30–90 seconds of degraded service) exactly before the most critical trading period. JIT compilation warm-up effects would cause elevated latency for 2–5 minutes after restart during peak load. This solves nothing and introduces new risks.

stages.principalRationale: In an incident, prefer the smallest change that removes the trigger. Raising the region size is one flag on the collector you already understand; changing collectors is a bigger decision that deserves a load test. Run JFR at the same time, because the lasting fix is in the code.

stages.question: JFR allocation profiling identifies the source: the payment authorisation service builds a JSON audit record per transaction, serialises it to a byte[], and sends it to the audit service. At peak load, audit records average 2.3MB each. What is the correct long-term fix?

options.label: A
options.text: Build the audit record on a background thread, so the large allocation still happens but no longer sits on the request path of the authorisation response.
options.feedback: Background threading removes the latency contribution but does not eliminate the humongous allocation. The byte[] is still created, still allocated in old gen by G1GC when it is large enough to be humongous. The allocation pressure problem remains, just shifted off the critical path. With the larger region size this is no longer an immediate problem, but under extreme load the allocation rate still matters.

options.label: B
options.text: Stream the JSON straight to the HTTP output stream (writeValue(OutputStream)) instead of writeValueAsBytes(), so no large byte[] is built. Confirm with JFR.
options.feedback: Correct. The root cause is buffering the entire JSON payload into a byte[] before sending. Streaming serialisation writes directly to the HTTP output buffer in chunks — no large intermediate byte[] is ever allocated. This eliminates the humongous allocation entirely, not just for G1GC but for all future GC algorithms. JFR verification closes the loop: confirms the fix worked and the allocation profile is clean. This is defensive engineering: eliminate the problem class, not just mitigate it.

options.label: C
options.text: GZIP the audit record before sending it. JSON usually compresses about 10:1, so the 2.3 MB record becomes about 230 KB — well below the humongous threshold.
options.feedback: Compression reduces the final size but requires allocating the uncompressed byte[] first, compressing it into a new byte[] second. The peak allocation is still > 2MB during the compression process. The compressed output may be below the humongous threshold, but the intermediate uncompressed buffer is still humongous. Streaming compression (GZIPOutputStream wrapping the OutputStream) would address this — but the streaming serialisation approach is cleaner and avoids the CPU cost of compression.

options.label: D
options.text: Split each audit record into three parts under 1 MB and send them as three separate HTTP requests, so no single buffer reaches the humongous threshold.
options.feedback: Splitting one audit record into three sends three times the HTTP overhead, triples the number of write transactions at the audit service, and complicates audit record reconstruction. This creates correctness risk (what if 1 of 3 sends fails?) for a problem that has a clean solution at the allocation level.

stages.principalRationale: The correct fix eliminates the allocation, not just its GC classification. Streaming serialisation is a standard pattern for large payload handling in financial APIs: write to the output stream as the object graph is traversed, never materialise the whole payload in memory. This pattern also reduces memory pressure on the receiving end.

debrief.summary: At market-open load, 2.3 MB audit buffers were humongous objects in G1 (4 MB regions → 2 MB threshold). They fragmented the old generation until G1 could not find free regions and fell back to multi-second Full GCs. The quick, low-risk mitigation is a larger region size; the lasting fix is streaming serialisation so the large buffers are never created.
keyTakeaways: G1 humongous threshold = half the region size (4 MB regions → 2 MB objects)
Humongous objects need contiguous old-gen regions and fragment the heap
Raising G1HeapRegionSize is a one-flag mitigation; changing collector needs testing
JFR allocation profiling finds the exact code creating large objects
Streaming serialisation removes the large intermediate byte[] altogether
furtherReading: Oracle — HotSpot Virtual Machine Garbage Collection Tuning Guide: G1 humongous objects
JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) documentation — allocation profiling

scenarios.title: The Phantom Trade
scenarios.subtitle: Database Isolation Failure in FX Exposure Limit Enforcement
scenarios.context:
An FX trading system enforces a £500,000 maximum exposure per trader per currency pair per day. The check runs as: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM fx_positions WHERE trader_id = ? AND currency_pair = ? AND trade_date = CURRENT_DATE. If sum + new_trade_amount <= 500,000, the trade is accepted and a new row is inserted into fx_positions.

At 10:03:17.421 the same trader submits two GBP/USD trades of £450,000 each from two terminals, and they are handled by two different pods. Both requests read an exposure of £0, both pass the check, and both rows are inserted. Exposure is now £900,000 — £400,000 over the limit. Compliance is alerted at 10:04. No error was logged.
systemConstraints: PostgreSQL 16, READ COMMITTED isolation (default)
fx_positions: (id, trader_id, currency_pair, amount, trade_date, created_at) — one row per trade
The two requests ran on different pods within the same millisecond
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE cannot be used with SUM(), and there were no rows to lock anyway (£0 exposure)
Trades can later be amended or cancelled

stages.question: What kind of concurrency anomaly allowed this breach?

options.label: A
options.text: Write skew via a phantom: each checked a SUM over rows not yet inserted, then inserted a row the other could not see. No shared row — nothing to lock or conflict on.
options.feedback: Correct. Each transaction read the set of matching rows (empty, so SUM = £0) and then inserted a new row into that set. Neither insert changes a row the other transaction read, so READ COMMITTED sees no conflict, and there is no existing row that SELECT ... FOR UPDATE could lock. The invariant "SUM ≤ £500,000" is about a set of rows, and checking it safely needs either a single row that represents the set or an isolation level that detects this pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: A lost update: both transactions read £0 and then overwrote the same exposure row with £450,000, so one write was silently lost, as in a classic read-modify-write race.
options.feedback: Not quite. A lost update happens when two transactions overwrite the same row. Here there is no shared row: each trade inserts its own new row. The rule that broke is a condition over a set of rows (the SUM), which is a write-skew / phantom problem.

options.label: C
options.text: A dirty read: the second transaction read the first one's uncommitted £450,000 row, but a visibility bug made the aggregate return £0 instead of the pending amount.
options.feedback: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads by definition — it only returns committed data. There is no database bug here. Transaction 2 correctly returned £0 because Transaction 1 had not yet committed. The problem is that the check logic requires knowing about concurrent in-flight transactions, which READ COMMITTED cannot provide.

options.label: D
options.text: A network partition between the two pods: each pod had stale cached exposure data and could not see the other pod's in-progress trade until the partition healed.
options.feedback: Application pods do not communicate with each other about in-progress transactions — the database is the coordination point. A network partition between pods would not affect their independent connections to the same PostgreSQL instance. Both transactions execute correctly against the database; the problem is the database isolation level not preventing their concurrent execution.

stages.principalRationale: The invariant here is about a set of rows (a SUM), not a single row. Two transactions each insert a row the other cannot see, so no row-level conflict exists. Recognising write skew — and that FOR UPDATE cannot lock rows that do not exist yet — is the core insight.

stages.question: Which fix enforces the limit most reliably under concurrency?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to REPEATABLE READ. Each transaction then works on one snapshot taken at its start, which prevents phantom reads and therefore prevents the breach.
options.feedback: Wrong. In PostgreSQL, REPEATABLE READ gives each transaction a stable snapshot, but it does not detect write skew: both transactions still see £0 in their snapshots and both inserts still succeed. Only SERIALIZABLE (SSI) detects this pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the check and the insert under SERIALIZABLE isolation. PostgreSQL's SSI detects the conflict and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001, which the application must retry.
options.feedback: Correct but heavier. SSI does catch this write skew, so the limit holds. The costs: every code path must run at SERIALIZABLE and retry on 40001, SSI can also abort transactions that did not really conflict (false positives), and retry rates rise under load. It is a valid fix, but a dedicated exposure row is simpler and cheaper for a single, well-known invariant.

options.label: C
options.text: One exposure row per (trader, pair, day), updated with the trade: UPDATE ... SET used = used + :amt WHERE ... AND used + :amt <= 500000. 0 rows = reject.
options.feedback: Correct. The limit now lives in one row, so the database's ordinary row locking serialises exactly the trades that compete for the same limit — and nothing else. The check and the increment are one atomic statement, it works under READ COMMITTED, there are no retry storms, and the exposure value can be read directly by risk systems. Create the row with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING before the update.

options.label: D
options.text: Take a PostgreSQL advisory lock on hash(trader, pair, day) before the check, so that only one trade at a time can check and insert for the same limit.
options.feedback: This works only if every code path that books or amends a trade remembers to take the same lock. One missed path (a batch import, an amendment API) silently breaks the limit again. Putting the limit into a row makes the database enforce it everywhere.

stages.principalRationale: Turn the set invariant into a row invariant. One exposure row per limit lets ordinary row locking serialise exactly the competing trades, with a single atomic conditional UPDATE. SERIALIZABLE also works but costs retries and false aborts; advisory locks depend on every code path remembering them.

stages.question: You deploy the exposure row. Trades can later be amended or cancelled. How do you keep the exposure row correct over time?

options.label: A
options.text: Recalculate every exposure row from fx_positions once a night with a batch job, and overwrite the stored value with the recalculated SUM.
options.feedback: A nightly rebuild corrects drift eventually, but during the day the exposure can be wrong for hours — and a wrong-too-low exposure is exactly when a trader can breach the limit. Corrections must happen in the same transaction as the change.

options.label: B
options.text: Adjust the exposure row in the same transaction as each amendment or cancellation, and regularly check exposure = SUM(positions), alerting on any gap.
options.feedback: Correct. Every change to a position changes its exposure in the same transaction, so they can never disagree after a commit. The reconciliation check is the safety net: if any code path forgets to update the exposure row, the mismatch is detected and investigated quickly instead of being discovered by compliance.

options.label: C
options.text: Never reduce the exposure row: once a trade is booked, its amount stays counted even if it is cancelled, because that keeps the limit check on the safe side.
options.feedback: Safe for the limit but wrong for the business: cancelled trades keep using up the trader's limit, so legitimate trades are rejected later in the day. Exposure must reflect the real positions, both up and down.

options.label: D
options.text: Store the exposure in Redis with INCRBY/DECRBY for speed, and keep fx_positions in PostgreSQL as the record of trades.
options.feedback: This splits one invariant across two systems with no shared transaction. A crash between the PostgreSQL insert and the Redis increment leaves them inconsistent — the dual-write problem — and Redis is not the system of record for a regulatory limit.

stages.principalRationale: A derived value (exposure) must change in the same transaction as its source (positions), and a reconciliation check proves they still agree. This is the same pattern as balance vs. ledger entries in a double-entry system.

debrief.summary: Two trades each checked a SUM over rows that did not exist yet and each inserted a new row — write skew, which READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ do not prevent and FOR UPDATE cannot lock. The most reliable fix stores the exposure in one row per limit and updates it with an atomic conditional UPDATE in the same transaction as the trade, backed by a reconciliation check against the positions table.
keyTakeaways: Invariants over a set of rows (SUM, COUNT) are vulnerable to write skew
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks existing rows only — it cannot lock "no rows yet"
REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL does not prevent write skew; SERIALIZABLE does
Best practice: one row per limit + atomic conditional UPDATE
Update derived values in the same transaction as their source, and reconcile regularly
furtherReading: PostgreSQL documentation — Transaction Isolation: Serializable and serialization anomalies
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann), chapter 7 — Write skew and phantoms

scenarios.title: The Penny Drift
scenarios.subtitle: Floating-Point Money, Rounding and Fee Allocation
scenarios.context:
A multi-currency wallet converts balances between currencies and splits every merchant fee three ways: platform 50%, partner 30%, card network 20%. Finance runs month-end reconciliation and finds the general ledger is out of balance by £1,412.37. The difference is spread across 3.1 million FX conversions and fee splits; no single transaction is off by more than one or two pennies, and nothing failed or was logged.

The conversion service is written in Java. Amounts arrive as decimal strings, are parsed into `double`, multiplied by the FX rate (6 decimal places), rounded with `Math.round(x * 100) / 100.0`, and stored in PostgreSQL `NUMERIC(19,2)`. Each fee share is calculated and rounded on its own. The wallet also supports JPY (no minor unit) and KWD (three decimal places).
systemConstraints: Java 21 service: amounts held as double during conversion
FX rates: 6 decimal places, e.g. 0.787412
PostgreSQL: NUMERIC(19,2) for every currency
Fee split 50 / 30 / 20, each share rounded HALF_UP on its own
3.1M conversions and fee splits per month
Supported currencies include GBP, USD, EUR, JPY (0 decimals), KWD (3 decimals)

stages.question: Why does the ledger drift by small amounts, and what is the primary fix?

options.label: A
options.text: Stale FX rates: the rate cache refreshes every 60 seconds, so some conversions use a rate a few seconds old. Fix by refreshing rates on every request.
options.feedback: Rate freshness is a pricing question, not a ledger-balance one. Even with a stale rate, each conversion still posts matching debit and credit amounts, so the books would balance. The drift comes from how the amounts are calculated and rounded.

options.label: B
options.text: double cannot hold most decimal amounts exactly, and fee shares are rounded one by one so they do not always sum to the fee. Use BigDecimal or integer minor units, with explicit rounding.
options.feedback: Correct. Binary floating point cannot represent values such as 0.1 exactly, so every multiply-and-round on a double can land a penny off. Independent rounding of each fee share adds a second error: £0.05 split 50/30/20 gives 0.025 → 0.03, 0.015 → 0.02 and 0.01, which adds up to 0.06. Money must be held as BigDecimal (or as a long count of minor units) with an explicit scale and RoundingMode, and allocations must be designed so the parts always add up to the total.

options.label: C
options.text: PostgreSQL truncation: NUMERIC(19,2) silently drops the third decimal place on insert. Fix by changing the column to NUMERIC(19,6) so no precision is lost when amounts are stored.
options.feedback: PostgreSQL NUMERIC rounds (it does not silently truncate) to the column scale, and storing more decimals does not stop the shares from adding up to more or less than the total. It also breaks currencies that have a fixed number of minor units. The errors are created in the Java calculation, before the insert.

options.label: D
options.text: Month-end cut-off: conversions made around midnight are counted in both months by the reconciliation query. Fix by making the reconciliation window end-exclusive.
options.feedback: A cut-off error moves whole transactions between periods; it would not produce millions of one- and two-penny differences. The pattern of tiny, widespread differences points at arithmetic and rounding, not timing.

stages.principalRationale: Small, widespread, silent differences are the fingerprint of arithmetic errors, not of lost messages or timing. A Principal Engineer recognises that money needs a decimal type with explicit rounding rules, and that every split must be designed so the parts sum exactly to the whole — otherwise the ledger cannot balance by construction.

stages.question: A fee of £0.05 must be split 50 / 30 / 20 so that the three shares always add up exactly to the fee. Which allocation method do you choose?

options.label: A
options.text: Round every share with HALF_EVEN (banker's rounding) instead of HALF_UP. Rounding errors then cancel out on average across millions of transactions.
options.feedback: HALF_EVEN removes the upward bias of HALF_UP, so totals drift less — but it gives no guarantee for an individual split. Each split must add up exactly, every time; "correct on average" still leaves individual journal entries unbalanced.

options.label: B
options.text: Post the monthly difference to a "rounding differences" suspense account, so the ledger balances again without changing the fee calculation itself.
options.feedback: A suspense account makes the trial balance look right but hides the cause, and auditors will ask why it grows every month. It is acceptable only for small, documented, unavoidable differences — not as a substitute for correct allocation.

options.label: C
options.text: Calculate the first two shares with rounding, and give the third party "fee minus the other two". The shares add up, so no further logic is needed.
options.feedback: This balances, but it always pushes the full rounding error onto the last party, which is unfair and can even produce negative shares for small fees. Largest-remainder allocation balances and spreads the pennies fairly and predictably.

options.label: D
options.text: Largest remainder: give each party its rounded-down share in pennies, then hand out the leftover pennies to the largest remainders (fixed tie-break).
options.feedback: Correct. £0.05 = 5 pence: 50% = 2.5 → 2, 30% = 1.5 → 1, 20% = 1.0 → 1, total 4, one penny left over. The largest remainders are 0.5 (platform) and 0.5 (partner); with a fixed tie-break the penny goes to the platform, giving 3 + 1 + 1 = 5. Every split balances exactly, and the deterministic tie-break makes results repeatable for audits.

stages.principalRationale: Allocation is a solved problem: allocate whole minor units and distribute the remainder deterministically. The key insight is that "parts must sum to the whole" is an invariant you design for, not something you fix afterwards with suspense accounts.

stages.question: The wallet supports JPY (0 decimals) and KWD (3 decimals) as well as GBP and USD. How should amounts be represented and stored?

options.label: A
options.text: Store every amount as a long number of cents (amount × 100). Integers are exact and fast, and the same rule works for every currency in the system.
options.feedback: Integers are a good idea, but "× 100" is not: JPY has no minor unit and KWD has 1,000 fils to the dinar. A fixed factor stores KWD amounts with too little precision and JPY amounts with fake precision. The factor must come from the currency.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep NUMERIC(19,2) for all currencies and round JPY and KWD to two decimals at the API edge, so the database schema stays simple and uniform.
options.feedback: Two decimals is wrong for both: JPY 1,234.50 is not a valid amount, and KWD 1.234 would lose its third decimal. Each currency has its own number of minor units (ISO 4217) and the data model must respect it.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep amount and currency together; take scale from the currency's ISO 4217 minor units and use BigDecimal or a Money type in Java.
options.feedback: Correct. An amount is meaningless without its currency, and the currency defines the valid scale: 0 for JPY, 2 for GBP, 3 for KWD. Validate incoming scale against the currency, round only with an explicit RoundingMode, and keep amount and currency together in one value type (for example JSR 354 / Moneta, or your own Money class).

options.label: D
options.text: Keep amounts as strings end to end, exactly as received from clients, and only convert them to numbers when a calculation is needed.
options.feedback: Strings avoid floating-point errors in storage but push parsing, validation and rounding to every caller, and they cannot be summed or compared safely in SQL. Money needs a numeric decimal type plus the currency.

stages.principalRationale: A Principal Engineer models money as a value object — amount plus currency — and lets the currency define precision. Hard-coding "two decimals" or "× 100" is one of the most common and most expensive defects in payment systems once a new currency is added.

debrief.summary: The ledger drift had two arithmetic causes: double cannot represent decimal money exactly, and fee shares were rounded independently so they did not always sum to the fee. The fix is a decimal money type with explicit rounding, largest-remainder allocation so parts always add up to the whole, and a Money value type whose precision comes from the currency.
keyTakeaways: Never use float or double for money; use BigDecimal or integer minor units
Always round with an explicit scale and RoundingMode — never implicitly
Design splits so the parts sum exactly to the total (largest-remainder allocation)
A suspense account hides rounding defects; it does not fix them
Precision depends on the currency (ISO 4217): JPY 0, GBP 2, KWD 3
furtherReading: Martin Fowler — Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture: the Money pattern
JSR 354 (Java Money and Currency API) and its reference implementation Moneta
ISO 4217 — currency codes and minor units

scenarios.title: The Database Migration Deadline
scenarios.subtitle: DDL Lock Queues on a Live 800M-Row Table
scenarios.context:
Compliance needs a new column on `payment_transactions` (PostgreSQL 16, 800 million rows, 20,000 inserts per second). The migration is:

ALTER TABLE payment_transactions ADD COLUMN risk_score NUMERIC(5,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00;

In staging it finished in 40 ms. In production, at 10:05, it caused a 4-minute total outage of the payment API: every insert and every read on the table hung, connection pools filled up, and health checks failed. When the DBA killed the migration session, everything recovered within seconds.

pg_stat_activity during the incident showed a reporting query that had been reading `payment_transactions` for 3 hours, the ALTER TABLE waiting behind it, and about 2,000 application queries waiting behind the ALTER TABLE.
systemConstraints: PostgreSQL 16, 800M rows, ~20,000 inserts/second
Migration tool: Flyway, runs at application start-up
No lock_timeout or statement_timeout set for migrations
A 3-hour analytics query was running on the primary
Staging: same DDL finished in 40 ms

stages.question: The DDL took 40 ms in staging. Why did it stop all traffic on this table in production?

options.label: A
options.text: Adding a NOT NULL column with a default rewrites all 800M rows to store the new value. The rewrite holds an exclusive lock on the table for its whole duration, which blocks reads and writes.
options.feedback: This was true up to PostgreSQL 10. Since PostgreSQL 11, a constant default is stored once in the catalogue and no rows are rewritten — which is why staging took 40 ms. The outage was caused by waiting for the lock, not by doing work.

options.label: B
options.text: PostgreSQL must scan all 800M rows to verify the NOT NULL constraint before it commits, and it holds a SHARE lock during the scan that allows reads but blocks every insert.
options.feedback: With a constant non-null default, every existing row already satisfies NOT NULL through the stored default, so no validation scan is needed. Also, the incident blocked reads as well as writes, which a SHARE lock would not do.

options.label: C
options.text: All indexes on the table must be rebuilt so that they know about the new column, and the index rebuild blocks writes until it completes on every index.
options.feedback: Adding a column does not rebuild existing indexes; they do not contain the new column. The cause is the lock queue, not index maintenance.

options.label: D
options.text: The ALTER needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. It queued behind the 3-hour query, and every new query queued behind the ALTER — the DDL is instant, the wait was not.
options.feedback: Correct. Since PostgreSQL 11, adding a column with a constant default is a metadata-only change, so the DDL itself takes milliseconds. But it still needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which conflicts with every other lock, including the ACCESS SHARE lock held by the long-running report. PostgreSQL grants locks in queue order, so all new reads and writes lined up behind the waiting ALTER. The table was blocked for as long as the ALTER waited — not for as long as it ran.

stages.principalRationale: The lesson is that DDL risk is about locks, not only about duration. A Principal Engineer asks two questions about every migration: what lock does it need, and what could it end up waiting behind? A 40 ms change can still cause a multi-minute outage.

stages.question: How should this migration (and future DDL on hot tables) be run safely?

options.label: A
options.text: Give the migration a short lock_timeout (2–5 s) and retry with backoff, so it gives up instead of blocking everyone. Check for long transactions first.
options.feedback: Correct. With lock_timeout, the ALTER waits at most a few seconds for its lock; if it does not get it, it fails, the queue behind it is released, and the migration retries later. Checking pg_stat_activity for long-running transactions first (and moving long analytics queries to a replica) removes the usual blocker. Most production DDL incidents in PostgreSQL are lock-queue incidents, and this is the standard defence.

options.label: B
options.text: Use pg_repack to rebuild the table online with the new column. It copies rows in the background and needs only a brief exclusive lock at the end to swap the tables.
options.feedback: pg_repack is for reclaiming bloat; it is heavy for 800M rows and its final swap still needs an exclusive lock, which can queue in exactly the same way. The DDL itself is already instant — the problem to solve is how long it waits for its lock.

options.label: C
options.text: Run all schema changes in a monthly maintenance window at night, when traffic is low, and announce a short downtime for the payment API.
options.feedback: Planned downtime is avoidable here and expensive for a payment platform. Low traffic also does not help if a long nightly batch or report is holding a lock at that time. A lock timeout with retries protects you at any hour.

options.label: D
options.text: Build a second database, apply the DDL there, copy the data with logical replication, and switch the application to the new database when it has caught up.
options.feedback: A blue-green database switch is a large, risky project for what is a millisecond metadata change. The real issue is the lock queue, which a lock timeout solves directly.

stages.principalRationale: A lock timeout turns a potential outage into a failed, retryable migration. Combined with "no long transactions on the primary", it removes the most common cause of DDL incidents in PostgreSQL.

stages.question: Compliance now wants risk_score calculated for every existing row from other columns (not the constant 0.00). How do you backfill 800M rows without hurting production?

options.label: A
options.text: Run one statement — UPDATE payment_transactions SET risk_score = f(...) — in a single transaction. MVCC means readers are not blocked, so the update can run during the day.
options.feedback: A single UPDATE on 800M rows would hold a lock on each row as it is processed. While MVCC allows concurrent reads of old row versions, the UPDATE itself generates 800M row rewrites, saturates I/O, generates enormous WAL (so replicas fall far behind), and runs for hours. The absence of a table-level lock does not make this safe — the I/O impact would severely degrade the production system.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the backfill on a read replica so the primary is not affected, and promote the replica to primary once the backfill has finished.
options.feedback: Read replicas apply changes from the primary via WAL streaming — they cannot accept writes directly (unless promoted). Running writes on a read replica would require promoting it, which makes it the new primary and leaves the old primary as a detached standalone instance. This is not a backfill strategy — it is a failover, and would be catastrophic for data integrity.

options.label: C
options.text: Update in primary-key batches of 1,000–10,000 rows with a short pause, and pause automatically when replication lag or I/O go above agreed limits.
options.feedback: Correct. Small-batch updates with rate limiting give production traffic the I/O headroom to continue processing. The sleep interval is adjustable — pause more aggressively during peak hours, run faster during off-peak. Monitoring replication lag provides direct feedback: if lag increases, reduce batch rate. Online-migration tools such as gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change (for MySQL) use the same throttling idea.

options.label: D
options.text: Run the backfill with 8 parallel workers, each on its own primary-key range. Each worker's updates touch different rows, so they finish 8× faster without extra impact.
options.feedback: Parallelising with 8 workers multiplies I/O pressure 8×. The I/O impact is not independent per thread — all threads compete for the same disk bandwidth. 8 parallel workers would saturate I/O much faster than a single-threaded batcher and would likely push replication lag far beyond safe limits. Rate-limiting a single thread and monitoring lag is the correct approach; parallelism can be cautiously increased only if I/O headroom exists.

stages.principalRationale: Backfills are production workloads. Small batches keep each transaction and lock short, and the feedback loop on replication lag and I/O makes the job adapt to production load instead of fighting it.

debrief.summary: Modern PostgreSQL adds a column with a constant default instantly, but the ALTER still needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Waiting for that lock behind a long-running query blocked every query that arrived afterwards. Protect DDL with a short lock_timeout and retries, keep long transactions off the primary, and backfill large tables in small, throttled batches.
keyTakeaways: Since PostgreSQL 11, ADD COLUMN with a constant default does not rewrite the table
Every ALTER TABLE still needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — and waiting for it blocks everyone behind it
Always set lock_timeout (and statement_timeout) for migration sessions, and retry with backoff
Long-running transactions on the primary are the usual blocker; move analytics to replicas
Backfill in small primary-key batches with throttling and replication-lag checks
furtherReading: PostgreSQL documentation — Explicit Locking (table-level lock modes and conflicts)
PostgreSQL documentation — ALTER TABLE (notes on adding columns with defaults)

scenarios.title: The Reconciliation Break
scenarios.subtitle: Business-Day Cut-offs, Time Zones and Timing Breaks
scenarios.context:
Every night at 02:00 a reconciliation job matches the internal card ledger against the card scheme's settlement file for the previous business day. The scheme defines the business day in London local time. Reconciliation has been clean all summer.

Since the clocks went back on Sunday 26 October, reconciliation reports about 600 breaks every night, worth around £48,000. Half are ledger entries missing from the file and half are file entries missing from the ledger. Every break has a timestamp between 23:00 and 00:00 London time, and every one of them matches automatically the following night. Operations staff have started force-matching them by hand.

The ledger side selects transactions with: `created_at >= businessDate.atStartOfDay().atOffset(ZoneOffset.ofHours(1))` and `< businessDate.plusDays(1)...` — written in July.
systemConstraints: Ledger timestamps stored as timestamptz (UTC instants)
Scheme settlement file: business day = 00:00–24:00 London local time
Ledger window built with a fixed offset: ZoneOffset.ofHours(1)
Breaks: ~600/night, all between 23:00 and 00:00, all self-match next night
Matching key today: card, amount, business date

stages.question: What is causing the nightly breaks?

options.label: A
options.text: The ledger window uses a fixed +01:00 (summer time) offset. Since the clocks changed, London is +00:00, so 23:00–00:00 items fall into different days on each side.
options.feedback: Correct. ZoneOffset.ofHours(1) is only right during British Summer Time. From 26 October, London midnight is 00:00 UTC, but the ledger window still starts at 23:00 UTC. Items from 23:00–00:00 London time fall into the next day on the ledger side and the current day on the scheme side. They are timing breaks: no money is missing, which is why they all match the following night.

options.label: B
options.text: Lost Kafka events: some card transactions are not reaching the ledger in time and arrive a day late, so they appear as missing from the ledger until the next night's run.
options.feedback: Late or lost events would create breaks on one side only (in the file, missing from the ledger) and would not follow a clean 23:00–00:00 pattern starting on the night the clocks changed. Here breaks appear on both sides, in equal numbers, in one exact hour.

options.label: C
options.text: The scheme settlement file is being truncated during transfer, so the last hour of transactions is missing from the file and only arrives with the next day's file.
options.feedback: A truncated file would only cause "missing from file" breaks. The equal number of breaks on both sides, all in one hour, points to a boundary difference rather than missing data.

options.label: D
options.text: FX rounding differences: the scheme converts cross-border amounts with a different rounding rule, so the amounts do not match exactly and the items are reported as unmatched.
options.feedback: Rounding differences produce amount mismatches on the same transaction, spread across the whole day — not whole items missing on each side within one hour.

stages.principalRationale: Reading the shape of the breaks is the key skill: equal and opposite breaks, in one exact hour, starting on a clock-change date, and clearing the next day all point to a boundary definition, not to lost money. A Principal Engineer classifies breaks before fixing anything.

stages.question: Operations are force-matching breaks by hand. How should the reconciliation process treat breaks like these?

options.label: A
options.text: Let operations keep force-matching the items, but post an adjusting entry for each one so the ledger and the file agree for that business day.
options.feedback: Adjusting entries for items that are not really wrong create real ledger errors and double-count money when the items match naturally the next night. Manual force-matching also removes the evidence of the underlying defect.

options.label: B
options.text: Widen the matching window to ±24 hours on both sides, so items near the day boundary are always matched with each other in the same run.
options.feedback: This removes this symptom, but it also matches things it should not (for example a genuine duplicate the next day), and it hides boundary defects instead of reporting them. Tolerances should be explicit categories with ageing rules, not a wide net.

options.label: C
options.text: Exclude the 23:00–00:00 window from reconciliation until the time-zone code is fixed, because everything in that hour is known to match the next night anyway.
options.feedback: Excluding an hour of transactions means real breaks in that hour (fraud, duplicates, missing settlements) would go unnoticed. Reconciliation must cover 100% of items.

options.label: D
options.text: Match on stable keys (scheme reference, amount, currency), not dates. Classify: timing breaks carry forward and must clear by T+1; everything else goes to operations.
options.feedback: Correct. Matching on a stable reference rather than on a date makes the process robust to boundary differences. A timing category with an ageing rule means expected timing differences clear automatically while still being tracked, and anything that does not clear in time — or any amount difference — is escalated. Operations then spend their time only on real problems.

stages.principalRationale: Mature reconciliation separates matching from investigation: match on stable identifiers, classify breaks, and apply ageing rules. Timing breaks are normal around cut-offs; they become a problem only when they do not clear, and the process should make that visible automatically.

stages.question: How do you fix the time handling so this cannot happen at the next clock change?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch every server and database to UTC and define the business day as 00:00–24:00 UTC, so there are no clock changes to worry about at all.
options.feedback: Running infrastructure in UTC is good practice, but the business day is defined by the scheme in London time. A UTC day would still disagree with the file for half the year. Your window must match the counterparty's definition.

options.label: B
options.text: Store UTC instants, define the business day with ZoneId Europe/London (atStartOfDay(zone)), and test the 23-hour and 25-hour days.
options.feedback: Correct. A ZoneId carries the daylight-saving rules, so each day's start and end are calculated correctly, including the 23-hour day in March and the 25-hour day in October. Tests that cover both transition days lock the behaviour in, and making the cut-off zone and time configuration per counterparty supports schemes with different definitions.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the fixed offset but change it twice a year as part of the clock-change runbook: +01:00 in summer, +00:00 in winter.
options.feedback: A manual change twice a year will eventually be forgotten or done at the wrong time, and the clock-change nights themselves still need special handling. Time-zone rules belong in code and libraries, not in a runbook.

options.label: D
options.text: Store all timestamps as LocalDateTime in London time, so the ledger timestamps and the file timestamps can be compared directly without any conversion.
options.feedback: LocalDateTime has no zone or offset. During the October clock change the hour 01:00–02:00 happens twice, so two different instants get the same value and ordering becomes ambiguous. Store instants; apply zones only when defining business days or displaying times.

stages.principalRationale: Store instants, apply zones at the edges. Business days are defined by counterparties in their own time zones, and DST transitions produce 23- and 25-hour days. A Principal Engineer makes these rules explicit, configurable and tested rather than hard-coded.

debrief.summary: A fixed +01:00 offset, correct only in summer, shifted the ledger's business day by one hour after the clocks went back. The result was equal and opposite timing breaks in the 23:00–00:00 hour that cleared the next night. The fix is to define business days with a real time zone, match on stable references, and classify timing breaks with ageing rules instead of force-matching them.
keyTakeaways: A fixed offset is not a time zone; use ZoneId for anything that crosses DST changes
Store instants (UTC); apply time zones only to define business days or to display times
Match on stable identifiers, not on dates
Classify breaks (timing vs. real) and give timing breaks an ageing rule
Test cut-off logic on the 23-hour and 25-hour days
furtherReading: Java documentation — java.time: ZoneId, ZonedDateTime and ZoneOffset
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann), chapter 8 — unreliable clocks

scenarios.title: The Memory Leak
scenarios.subtitle: JVM OOM from Unbounded Cache Accumulating PDF Byte Arrays
scenarios.context:
Payment gateway pods restart every 4–6 hours with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. This started exactly 3 weeks ago after releasing a new PDF statement generation feature. Normal pod memory usage: 400MB. Pods restart at ~3.8GB heap used.

The team increased -Xmx from 2GB to 4GB two weeks ago, which extended pod lifetime from 2 hours to 4-6 hours without fixing the underlying issue. Kubernetes liveness probes restart pods on OOM, so availability is maintained (new pod starts in ~45 seconds). However, restarts coincide with peak transaction hours, causing elevated latency.
systemConstraints: Java 21, Spring Boot, -Xmx4g, G1GC
12 pods behind Kubernetes load balancer
PDF statement feature: generates account statements on demand via REST API GET /statements/{accountId}
JFR continuous recording enabled (default settings)
Heap dump on OOM: enabled (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError)
OOM heap dump size: 3.8GB — available in PersistentVolume
Memory growth: linear, ~600MB/hour at normal load

stages.question: Before analysing the heap dump, what is the most likely root cause based on the symptoms alone?

options.label: A
options.text: An unbounded cache added with the PDF feature: generated PDFs (byte[], ~2 MB each) are kept in a Map keyed by account with no size limit or expiry, so the heap fills over hours.
options.feedback: Correct. The pattern — linear memory growth starting exactly when a caching feature was released, dominated by byte[] in the heap dump — is the signature of an unbounded cache accumulating large objects. PDF byte arrays (~2MB each) with no eviction mean every unique account statement request adds 2MB permanently. After 3 weeks, tens of thousands of cached PDFs fill the heap. GC sees them as live objects (cache holds strong references) and cannot collect them.

options.label: B
options.text: A native memory leak in the PDF library: it allocates off-heap memory through JNI that the garbage collector never sees, so memory grows until the pod is killed.
options.feedback: Off-heap (native) memory leaks would manifest as pod-level memory exhaustion (Kubernetes OOMKill at the cgroup limit) without an OutOfMemoryError in JVM heap. The symptoms describe an OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space — this is an on-heap issue. If the GC cannot reclaim heap despite running, something is holding strong references to heap-allocated objects. Native memory leaks are a separate issue with different symptoms.

options.label: C
options.text: HTTP sessions from PDF downloads are never invalidated. Each session keeps a reference to the downloaded byte[] body, so every download stays in the heap until the session times out.
options.feedback: HTTP session accumulation is possible in stateful session-based applications, but modern Spring Boot REST APIs are typically stateless (no HttpSession per request). Session objects also don't directly hold response body byte[] — the response is sent to the client and the buffer is typically released after the response completes. The cache pattern is more consistent with the described symptoms.

options.label: D
options.text: The PDF feature creates a new ClassLoader per request to isolate the library, and those class loaders are never released, so Metaspace grows until the JVM fails.
options.feedback: ClassLoader leaks manifest as OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace (not heap space) and are associated with dynamic class loading patterns (OSGi, plugin architectures, hot deployment). The error message 'Java heap space' specifically indicates heap exhaustion, not Metaspace. Additionally, new ClassLoaders per request is an unusual and extreme design choice unlikely in a standard PDF library integration.

stages.principalRationale: Symptom pattern recognition: (1) OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space means strong references are preventing GC — not an off-heap problem; (2) linear growth that started with a known feature release means that feature introduced the growing reference; (3) the feature produces large objects (PDFs of about 2 MB). Together these strongly suggest an unbounded cache of large objects.

stages.question: You open the OOM heap dump in Eclipse MAT. What analysis steps confirm the root cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the Leak Suspects report and trust its first suspect. It names the leaking class and the code that filled it, so no further manual analysis is needed.
options.feedback: Eclipse MAT's Leak Suspects report is a useful starting point, but it performs heuristic analysis and may not identify the specific cache class clearly. It identifies 'accumulation points' by finding objects that retain large amounts of heap but cannot give the full context of why they are retained. The dominator tree analysis is more precise and actionable for cache-type leaks.

options.label: B
options.text: Open the Histogram sorted by shallow heap. byte[] will be at the top, and its total count and size confirm that byte arrays are what fills the heap.
options.feedback: The Histogram confirms byte[] accumulation (useful as a first validation step) but does not explain WHY the byte[] objects are retained. Without the Dominator Tree and GC Root analysis, you know what is using memory but not what is holding it live. The Dominator Tree is the tool that shows the retention chain and identifies the fix location.

options.label: C
options.text: Search the dump for known cache classes (ConcurrentHashMap, Guava, Caffeine). Any instance that retains more than 100 MB is the leaking cache.
options.feedback: Searching for specific cache class instances is a reasonable manual investigation step but requires knowing which cache libraries are in use and searching each one individually. The Dominator Tree approach is more systematic — it surfaces the largest memory holders regardless of their class type, without requiring prior knowledge of the caching mechanism used.

options.label: D
options.text: Dominator Tree by retained heap: inspect the top object, then "Path to GC Roots" on a sample byte[] to confirm the chain from GC root to cache.
options.feedback: Correct. The Dominator Tree identifies the largest retained-heap objects. For a cache leak, the cache object (HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap) will appear near the top, retaining a large fraction of total heap. 'Path to GC Roots' traces exactly why a specific byte[] is not collectable: the reference chain from the GC root (static field, Spring singleton bean) through the cache to the byte[]. This gives you the class name, field name, and code location to fix.

stages.principalRationale: Dominator Tree + Path to GC Roots is the standard methodology for heap dump analysis. The Dominator Tree identifies what is retaining the most memory; Path to GC Roots shows why it cannot be collected. Together they provide the class name, field name, and reference chain needed for a targeted fix.

stages.question: The analysis confirms: `PdfStatementService` has a static `Map<String, byte[]> statementCache` with no size limit. What is the correct fix and prevention strategy?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove the cache completely and generate the PDF on every request. Generation is mostly I/O, and the statements are rarely downloaded more than once.
options.feedback: Removing the cache is safe from a memory perspective but may introduce unacceptable latency for repeated requests. If PDF generation involves multiple database queries and report rendering (typical), uncached generation on every request could add 500ms–2s per call. Whether this is acceptable depends on the SLO. Caffeine with bounded size and TTL is better: it preserves performance benefit while adding safety bounds.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the Map but store WeakReference<byte[]> values, so the garbage collector can reclaim the PDF bytes automatically whenever memory gets tight.
options.feedback: WeakReferences allow GC to reclaim the referenced objects under memory pressure — but only after a full GC cycle determines memory is needed. In practice, WeakReference caches perform poorly: under steady load, GC constantly collects the cache entries (causing cache misses) or fails to collect fast enough under sudden load spikes (OOM still occurs). SoftReference (collected only before OOM) is better than WeakReference for caches, but Caffeine with explicit size limits is better than either reference type approach.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise -Xmx to 16 GB. Once every account's statement has been generated once, the cache stops growing and memory use becomes stable.
options.feedback: Increasing heap without fixing the unbounded cache is a time-delay, not a fix. New accounts are constantly added; existing account statements may be regenerated due to new transactions. The cache will grow without bound regardless of heap size. This was already demonstrated by the team's previous increase from 2GB to 4GB — it only extended the OOM interval.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace the static Map with a bounded Caffeine cache (byte-based maximumWeight + expireAfterAccess), and add a heap-usage alert.
options.feedback: Correct. A Caffeine cache with a byte-based maximumWeight (a weigher that returns each array's length, e.g. a 200 MB limit) and expireAfterAccess evicts by size and by idle time. Memory use now has a hard upper limit, while frequently requested statements stay fast. Replace the static field with a cache injected as a Spring @Bean, and add a heap-usage alert so any future growth is noticed long before an OutOfMemoryError.

stages.principalRationale: Every cache in production must have an explicit maximum size and TTL. These are not performance optimisations — they are correctness constraints that prevent memory exhaustion. Caffeine is the standard Java caching library that provides both. The fix takes under 10 lines of code; the prevention strategy is a code review policy requiring all caches to have bounded configuration.

debrief.summary: Unbounded caches accumulating large objects are one of the most common causes of Java OOM in production. The diagnostic path is: OOM error → heap dump → Dominator Tree → Path to GC Roots. The fix is to give the cache an explicit size bound and expiry, for example with Caffeine. Prevention is a code review policy requiring bounded configuration on all caches.
keyTakeaways: OOM: Java heap space → strong references preventing GC, not off-heap native memory
Dominator Tree identifies the largest retained-heap holders; Path to GC Roots shows why they cannot be collected
Every production cache needs a size bound (maximumSize or maximumWeight) and an expiry — no unbounded Maps
Caffeine is the standard Java cache: Caffeine.newBuilder().maximumWeight(bytes).weigher(...).expireAfterAccess(...).build()
Increasing heap without fixing the cache is a time-delay, not a solution
furtherReading: Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT) documentation — Dominator Tree and Paths to GC Roots
Caffeine documentation — Eviction by size and weight

scenarios.title: The Alert Fatigue
scenarios.subtitle: 420 PagerDuty Pages in One Week Hide a Real Outage
scenarios.context:
The payment processing team receives 420 PagerDuty pages in one week. 65% are P2 alerts for P99 latency > 500ms. P50 latency is healthy at 45ms. P99 is naturally spiky — GC pauses and 1–2% of slow downstream API calls push individual requests above 500ms even during normal operation.

Engineers begin muting P99 alerts during business hours. On Wednesday afternoon, a genuine 25-minute partial outage (40% of payments timing out) goes undetected for 25 minutes because the alert was lost in the noise. Customers escalate via Twitter. The engineering VP asks for a root-cause analysis of the monitoring failure.
systemConstraints: SLO: P99 latency < 200ms, 99.9% availability (monthly)
Current alert: P99 > 500ms for 1 consecutive minute → PagerDuty P2
Normal P99: 85ms median, spikes to 400-600ms for 2-3% of 1-minute windows
Outage P99: > 2,000ms for 25 consecutive minutes
Monthly error budget: 43.8 minutes of SLO-breaching downtime
Alert volume: 420 pages/week (65% false positive P99 alerts)
Prometheus + Grafana monitoring stack

stages.question: What is the fundamental flaw in the current alerting strategy that causes both the false positive storm and the missed real outage?

options.label: A
options.text: The 500 ms threshold is too low. Raising it to 2,000 ms removes the noisy pages and would still have caught the real outage, where P99 stayed above 2 seconds.
options.feedback: Raising the threshold to 2,000ms would have caught Wednesday's outage (P99 > 2,000ms) but would miss slower degradations that still breach the SLO. More importantly, threshold-based alerts on P99 have an inherent false positive rate due to natural variability — raising the threshold just shifts the threshold, it does not solve the underlying problem of threshold alerts not distinguishing transient spikes from sustained degradation.

options.label: B
options.text: P99 is the wrong indicator. P50 is much more stable, so alerting on median latency would remove the false positives and still catch a large outage.
options.feedback: P50 alerting would miss the 2% of slow requests that breach the SLO — it would not have caught Wednesday's outage (40% of payments timing out) until P50 was affected. SLOs are defined on the percentile that matters for user experience; dropping to P50 for alerting would create a monitoring gap for the slower tail of the distribution.

options.label: C
options.text: Too many people receive each page. Routing the alert only to the primary on-call engineer would reduce the feeling of noise and keep pages from being ignored.
options.feedback: Alert routing affects who receives pages but not the number of pages generated. Even if only one engineer is paged, 420 pages/week is alert fatigue — the volume is the problem, not the distribution. The fix must reduce the number of alerts generated by improving the alerting strategy, not just narrow the recipient list.

options.label: D
options.text: A point-in-time threshold pages once for a 1-minute blip and once for a 25-minute outage. It ignores how fast the error budget burns, so noise and outages look the same.
options.feedback: Exactly right. This is the fundamental problem with threshold alerting on point-in-time metrics. The alert does not encode the budget burn rate — it fires identically for a 1-minute spike and a 25-minute outage. The result is high false positive rate (spikes are common) with no additional urgency for genuine outages (same alert severity). Multi-window burn rate alerting solves this by linking alert severity to the rate of budget consumption.

stages.principalRationale: The core insight: threshold alerts fire on events, not on sustained budget burn. For SLO-based monitoring, what matters is not whether the SLO was briefly breached but how fast the error budget is being consumed. Multi-window burn rate alerting encodes this by measuring burn rate over both short and long windows simultaneously.

stages.question: What alerting strategy should replace the point-in-time P99 threshold alert?

options.label: A
options.text: Drop latency alerts and alert only on HTTP 5xx rate above 1%. Errors are a clearer signal than latency, and timeouts will show up as errors anyway.
options.feedback: Error rate alerting is complementary to latency alerting but does not replace it. Many SLO-violating scenarios produce timeouts (long latency) without 5xx errors — the client gives up and the server returns 200 OK too slowly. Wednesday's outage (40% payments timing out) may have shown as timeouts before error responses. SLO definitions should include both error rate and latency as SLIs.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the P99 alert but require it to stay above 500 ms for 15 consecutive minutes before paging, so short spikes are ignored.
options.feedback: 15-minute sustained alerting would have caught Wednesday's 25-minute outage (barely — it fires at minute 15 of 25). But it would still generate false positives on any 15-minute degradation period. More importantly, a 15-minute detection delay for major outages is too slow for a payment system — the SLO budget for a 15-minute delay is 15/43.8 = 34% consumed before alerting. Multi-window burn rate provides both fast detection for severe outages and slow detection for gradual degradation.

options.label: C
options.text: Multi-window burn-rate alerts: page only when the budget burns fast in both a short (1 h) and a long (6 h) window. Blips do not page; sustained burns do.
options.feedback: Correct. Multi-window burn rate alerting (from the Google SRE Workbook) uses two alert conditions: fast burn (1-hour window, high burn rate threshold — catches major outages quickly) and slow burn (6-hour window, lower burn rate threshold — catches sustained partial degradation). Both must fire simultaneously to page. A transient 2-minute spike burns fast in the 1h window but not in the 6h window — no page. Wednesday's 25-minute outage (40% timeout) burns fast in both windows — page. This directly solved the false positive problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Use anomaly detection: page when P99 is more than 3 standard deviations away from its rolling 7-day average, so the alert adapts to normal variation.
options.feedback: Anomaly detection is useful for capacity planning and trend analysis but is a poor fit for SLO-based alerting. It requires significant historical data for calibration, can mask seasonal patterns as 'normal', and does not encode the budget burn concept. A 3σ deviation on a naturally variable metric like P99 tail latency produces many false positives or misses genuine outages that happen to fit the historical pattern.

stages.principalRationale: Multi-window burn rate alerting is the Google SRE recommendation for SLO-based alerting. The dual-window requirement (both short and long windows must fire) is the key innovation — it filters transient spikes while catching both fast burns (major outages) and slow burns (gradual degradation). This directly addresses the false positive storm while maintaining genuine outage detection.

stages.question: With multi-window burn rate alerting in place, the team asks: when should a new feature deployment be blocked due to error budget status?

options.label: A
options.text: Never block deployments because of the error budget. Delivery and reliability are separate concerns, and the budget is only reviewed after releases.
options.feedback: If error budget is exhausted, every deployment that causes any additional unavailability exceeds the SLO commitment to customers. Deploying with zero remaining budget is a business decision — but it must be made explicitly, not by default. An error budget policy that blocks deployments when budget is low forces the team to treat availability as a first-class engineering metric, not an afterthought.

options.label: B
options.text: Block all deployments whenever less than 50% of the monthly budget remains and more than 15 days of the month are left.
options.feedback: A single 50% threshold is too conservative for most engineering teams — 50% budget with 15 days remaining means you are on track, not in trouble. Tiered thresholds (freely / caution / freeze) allow velocity to continue when the situation is not dire, while enforcing genuine caution when budget is critically low. A fixed 50% block would generate excessive friction and may cause teams to game the SLO definition.

options.label: C
options.text: Review the error budget in the weekly engineering meeting, and let the team vote on whether the next deployments should go ahead.
options.feedback: Weekly reviews are too infrequent for fast-moving deployment pipelines. Teams may deploy dozens of times per week. A documented, automatically enforceable policy (checked in CI/CD gate) is more robust than a weekly meeting. The policy should be consistent and predictable, not subject to weekly team votes.

options.label: D
options.text: A written error-budget policy: deploy normally with plenty of budget, add safeguards as it shrinks, freeze non-critical changes when it is nearly spent.
options.feedback: Correct. The error budget policy converts the abstract SLO budget into concrete deployment decisions. It aligns product velocity (want to ship features) with reliability (must maintain SLO). Crucially, it is documented and enforced — not ad hoc. When budget is low, the team naturally pivots to reliability work (which is what the SLO framework is designed to incentivise). The tiered policy (50% / 10% / 0%) balances velocity preservation with risk management.

stages.principalRationale: Error budget policy is what transforms SLOs from abstract metrics into engineering team behaviour. The tiered policy (freely / caution / freeze / stop) is the standard Google SRE pattern. The key benefit: the team self-regulates deployment velocity based on reliability evidence, without requiring management intervention.

debrief.summary: Alert fatigue is a monitoring system failure, not a human failure. Point-in-time threshold alerts fire identically for transient spikes and genuine outages, creating signal-to-noise ratios that make monitoring useless. Multi-window burn rate alerting links alert severity to error budget consumption rate — only paging when the SLO is being meaningfully breached. The error budget policy operationalises the SLO into deployment decisions.
keyTakeaways: Point-in-time threshold alerts cannot distinguish transient spikes from sustained outages
Multi-window burn rate: page when budget burns fast in BOTH 1h window AND 6h window simultaneously
Fast burn catches major outages (P1); slow burn catches gradual degradation (P2)
Error budget policy converts abstract SLO budget into concrete deployment gate decisions
Alert fatigue → engineers mute alerts → real outages missed: a predictable, preventable failure mode
furtherReading: Google — The Site Reliability Workbook, chapter 5: Alerting on SLOs
Google — Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 3: Embracing Risk (error budgets)

scenarios.title: The Config Disaster
scenarios.subtitle: Copy-Paste Error in Deployment Pipeline Causes 12,000 False Declines
scenarios.context:
At 09:12 on Monday, 12,000 customers are declined for payments in 45 minutes. The decline reason: FRAUD_SCORE_THRESHOLD_EXCEEDED. The fraud team investigates: `fraud_score_threshold` config changed from 0.75 to 0.075 in the last deployment. 99.8% of transactions score above 0.075 and are declined.

Root cause trace: a developer copy-pasted deployment config between environments. The staging config uses 0.075 (a testing value for triggering fraud alerts on test transactions). Production was supposed to retain 0.75. The copy-paste was not reviewed because config changes were bundled with the code change PR. No automated validation checked the config range before deployment.
systemConstraints: fraud_score_threshold: externally configured via Spring application.yml in the deployment artifact
Deployment: Kubernetes rolling deployment, all 12 pods updated within 4 minutes
Monitoring: fraud decline rate alert fires at > 5% decline rate. At 09:12, rate jumped to 99.8%.
Alert fired at 09:17 (5-minute evaluation window). Team diagnosed and rolled back by 09:57.
12,000 false declines in 45 minutes
Config is part of the application container image (baked in at build time)
No config schema validation step in CI/CD pipeline

stages.question: What are the two root causes of this incident — one technical, one process — and which is more important to fix first?

options.label: A
options.text: Technical: the threshold is hard-coded and should live in a database so it can be changed without a deployment. Process: developers need more training on configuration.
options.feedback: Database-driven configuration adds complexity and a new failure mode (database unavailable = service cannot start). Training is a low-leverage fix for a systematic process gap — the same error can be made by any developer, regardless of training. The technical root cause is lack of config validation; the process root cause is config and code bundled in the same review.

options.label: B
options.text: Technical: the alert window of 5 minutes was too slow to catch the decline spike. Process: someone should watch the dashboards during every deployment.
options.feedback: The 5-minute alert window is a valid concern (it contributed to 5 minutes of additional exposure before detection) but is not the root cause. Even a 1-minute alert would still have allowed about 270 false declines (12,000 in 45 minutes) before detection. The root cause is that an invalid config value was deployed — faster detection reduces impact but does not prevent the incident. Config validation prevents it entirely.

options.label: C
options.text: Technical: all 12 pods were replaced within 4 minutes, which is too fast. Process: post-deployment checks should confirm the decline rate before the rollout finishes.
options.feedback: Slower rollout reduces impact (fewer pods affected before detection) and post-deployment verification is valuable — but neither addresses the root cause: an invalid config value entered the deployment artifact. Post-deployment verification is a mitigation; config schema validation is prevention. For a payment system, even 1 pod with an invalid fraud threshold causes unacceptable false declines.

options.label: D
options.text: Technical: no validation (0.075 is outside 0.5–1.0). Process: the config change hid inside a code PR. Fix validation first — machines catch it every time.
options.feedback: Correct on both counts and the prioritisation. Config schema validation is the technical control that prevents out-of-range values regardless of human error. Separating config changes from code changes (or requiring separate review) is the process control that increases scrutiny. Schema validation catches what humans miss; process separation ensures humans look. Technical controls scale better than process controls — schema validation catches every future typo, training cannot.

stages.principalRationale: Root cause analysis must distinguish between causes (what allowed the error to occur) and mitigations (what limited its impact). Config schema validation is a cause-level fix: it prevents invalid values from being deployed. Alert speed and rollout speed are impact-limitation controls. Fix the cause first.

stages.question: What is the most effective technical control to prevent invalid config values from reaching production?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the values to a ConfigMap or secrets store owned by the platform team, so every change needs a separate ticket and a second person's approval.
options.feedback: Separating config ownership (platform team approves config changes) adds a human review gate. Human gates slow down the deployment pipeline and do not scale — the platform team becomes a bottleneck. Human reviewers also miss errors that schema validation would catch (the platform team reviewer may not know that 0.075 is invalid for fraud_score_threshold). Schema validation provides stronger guarantees with less process overhead.

options.label: B
options.text: Validate the value at application start-up (@Validated properties or a check in @PostConstruct) and refuse to start if the threshold is outside 0.5–1.0.
options.feedback: Application startup validation is better than no validation — it prevents the pod from starting with an invalid config, which is better than deploying and causing false declines. However, Kubernetes rolling deployment would launch the new pod, it would fail to start, Kubernetes would detect the crash loop and stop the rollout, and the existing pods (with the old config) would continue serving traffic. This catches the error at deployment time — but CI validation catches it even earlier (before the image is even built), which is better.

options.label: C
options.text: Config as code with a machine-checked schema (type, minimum 0.5, maximum 1.0) validated in CI before the image is built. An out-of-range value fails the build.
options.feedback: Correct. Config schema validation in CI is the technical control that closes the gap: it catches invalid values before the image is built, let alone deployed. The schema is source-controlled alongside the config (config-as-code), so the range constraint is visible to developers and enforced automatically. This catches typos, copy-paste errors, and value range errors that human reviewers miss. For financial config values (thresholds, limits, rate limits), schema validation is mandatory.

options.label: D
options.text: Encrypt the configuration values so that only the production pipeline can read them, which stops staging values being copied into production by mistake.
options.feedback: Encryption prevents viewing config values but does not prevent deploying wrong values. A developer who encrypts 0.075 with the production key has successfully deployed an invalid value that is now encrypted. Encryption addresses confidentiality, not config value correctness.

stages.principalRationale: Shift config validation left: catch errors in CI before the image is built, not after deployment when customers are affected. Schema-defined constraints for business-critical config values (thresholds, limits) are non-negotiable in financial systems.

stages.question: Config validation is in place. What deployment pattern provides the fastest detection of any unexpected production behaviour (including config values that pass schema validation but are still wrong)?

options.label: A
options.text: Blue-green: deploy to a second environment, run smoke tests, then switch all traffic at once — and switch back if something goes wrong.
options.feedback: Blue-green eliminates gradual rollout risk but puts all traffic onto the new version simultaneously after the switch. If the smoke tests miss the config issue (which is likely for edge cases), 100% of traffic is affected from the first second of the switch. It also requires running two full production environments simultaneously, which doubles infrastructure cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Canary: 1% of traffic to the new version, compare decline rates with the old one, roll back automatically on a clear difference, then widen step by step.
options.feedback: Correct. A canary deployment limits the blast radius of any undiscovered issue to the canary traffic percentage (1% → 12,000 customers becomes 120 customers). The automated comparison (canary decline rate vs. baseline) catches statistical anomalies in the new version without requiring engineers to manually interpret dashboards. Progressive rollout (1% → 10% → 25% → 100%) with automated gates is the industry-standard deployment pattern for high-risk production changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Feature flag: ship the new config switched off, enable it for 0.1% of users, and watch the results for 24 hours before enabling it for everyone.
options.feedback: Feature flags for config values are complex to implement correctly (the flag logic must be in the fraud service, not just the config) and 24-hour monitoring windows significantly slow deployment velocity. For a config value like a fraud threshold, a canary deployment achieves the same safety goal with a 15-minute observation window rather than 24 hours.

options.label: D
options.text: Shadow mode: run the new scoring next to the old one for an hour, log both decisions, and release only if they agree within 2%.
options.feedback: Shadow mode (dual-running and comparing results) is excellent for ML model validation and algorithm changes. For a config value change (threshold adjustment), it is overkill — the purpose of changing the threshold is precisely to change the decision rate. A shadow comparison would flag the threshold change as a 'mismatch' and block the deployment even when the change is intentional. Canary with business metric monitoring is more appropriate.

stages.principalRationale: Canary deployments limit blast radius while providing real production signal. The comparison-based automated gate (canary vs baseline) is what distinguishes a good canary from a simple gradual rollout — it surfaces problems without requiring manual interpretation. For financial services where configuration errors can cause thousands of customer-impacting decisions in minutes, canary with automated comparison is the deployment safety standard.

debrief.summary: Configuration errors are a leading cause of production incidents in modern deployment pipelines. The defence-in-depth approach: (1) schema validation in CI catches invalid values before the image is built; (2) application startup validation catches values that pass schema but fail business rules; (3) canary deployment limits blast radius for anything that passes both validation layers. Schema validation is the highest-leverage control — it scales automatically to every deployment.
keyTakeaways: Config schema validation in CI is the highest-leverage control: catches errors before the image is built
Config-as-code: define allowed ranges/values in a schema that is source-controlled and machine-validated
Application @PostConstruct validation is a secondary defence for business-rule constraints not expressible in schema
Canary deployment with automated comparison (canary vs baseline) limits blast radius to 1% of users
Never bundle config changes with code changes in the same PR — config changes deserve separate scrutiny
furtherReading: Google — The Site Reliability Workbook, chapter 16: Canarying Releases
Spring Boot documentation — @ConfigurationProperties validation

scenarios.title: The Slow Query Bomb
scenarios.subtitle: Billing Job Takes 4 Minutes in Staging, 6+ Hours in Production
scenarios.context:
The monthly billing job runs fine in staging: 50,000 customers, completes in 4 minutes. First production run with 8.2 million customers has been running for 6 hours without completing. The core query:

```sql
SELECT c.id, c.email, SUM(t.amount) as total_billed
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN transactions t ON c.id = t.customer_id
WHERE t.created_at >= '2026-10-01'
  AND c.billing_status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.id, c.email
```

Staging and production have identical schemas. The query runs in 4 minutes against the 50k staging dataset. The DBA ran EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on production and found: Seq Scan on transactions (cost=0 rows=312,847,000). No index is being used for the join or date filter.
systemConstraints: customers table: 8.2M rows (production), 50k rows (staging)
transactions table: 312M rows (production), 1.5M rows (staging)
Existing indexes: customers(id) PRIMARY KEY, transactions(id) PRIMARY KEY, customers(billing_status)
No index on transactions(customer_id) or transactions(created_at)
PostgreSQL query planner statistics: last ANALYZE ran 3 days ago on production
Staging: PostgreSQL shares same instance, different database, full ANALYZE runs nightly
transactions table size: ~160GB

stages.question: Why did the same query perform acceptably in staging but catastrophically in production?

options.label: A
options.text: Production is busy with OLTP traffic, so the billing query is starved of I/O bandwidth and runs far slower than it does on the quiet staging database.
