options.feedback: Concurrent load adds some I/O contention, but it cannot explain a 90× difference (4 minutes vs 6+ hours). The EXPLAIN output shows a full sequential scan of 312M rows — that volume of work, not contention, explains the difference.

options.label: B
options.text: Production has a lower max_parallel_workers_per_gather setting, which turns off the parallel query execution that made the same query fast in staging.
options.feedback: Parallel query settings affect speed but cannot explain a 90× difference on their own. Even with parallel workers, a 160GB sequential scan takes a long time. The real issue is that no index lets the query read only October's rows, so the whole table is scanned.

options.label: C
options.text: The production transactions table is not partitioned, so the billing scan suffers from table bloat and lock contention with the inserts running at the same time.
options.feedback: Partitioning would help this query significantly (partition pruning on created_at) but its absence does not explain the staging vs production difference — staging also has an unpartitioned transactions table. The difference is the data volume and the absence of a suitable index.

options.label: D
options.text: Same plan in both: a full scan of transactions. On 1.5M rows that is seconds; on 312M rows (160 GB) with no index for the date range, it reads everything and spills to disk.
options.feedback: Correct. Staging and production have the same schema and no index on transactions(customer_id) or (created_at), so the planner has only one option in both: a sequential scan of the whole table plus a hash join and aggregation. At staging size that is cheap. At production size it reads about 160 GB, and grouping 8.2M customers exceeds work_mem and spills to disk. Staging was simply too small to show the problem. (Note also that the WHERE condition on t.created_at turns the LEFT JOIN into an inner join, so customers without transactions are silently dropped — a correctness issue to raise with the billing team.)

stages.principalRationale: Query cost depends on data volume. A plan that is harmless on a small dataset can be catastrophic on a large one, so plans must be checked against production-sized data. EXPLAIN shows the plan; timings on small data prove nothing.

stages.question: What index strategy resolves the immediate problem, and what longer-term architectural change should be considered?

options.label: A
options.text: Composite index on transactions(customer_id, created_at). It matches the join column first and then the date, so each customer's October rows can be found directly.
options.feedback: Useful for per-customer lookups, but billing needs October rows for all 8.2M customers. Using this index means 8.2M separate index probes; the planner will often still prefer a full scan. Leading with created_at lets the query read just the October range.

options.label: B
options.text: Partition the transactions table by month now. The billing query then benefits from partition pruning and only scans the October partition.
options.feedback: Partitioning is an excellent long-term architectural improvement — it enables partition pruning (only scanning the relevant month's data) and simplifies data retention. However, partitioning a 160GB live table is a multi-hour online migration project, not an immediate fix. An index can be added with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (non-blocking) much sooner, restoring acceptable performance while partitioning is planned.

options.label: C
options.text: Run billing against a read replica with larger shared_buffers and work_mem, so it no longer competes with the OLTP workload on the primary.
options.feedback: Running analytics on a read replica is a good operational practice (reduces primary load), but it does not fix the missing index. The read replica has the same schema and the same absence of indexes — the same 160GB sequential scan would occur on the replica. Add the index first; then migrate to replica for operational isolation.

options.label: D
options.text: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on transactions(created_at) INCLUDE (customer_id, amount), then ANALYZE and check EXPLAIN. Longer term: monthly partitions.
options.feedback: Correct. Leading with created_at lets PostgreSQL read only October's rows, and INCLUDE (customer_id, amount) allows an index-only scan without touching the 160 GB heap. CONCURRENTLY builds it without blocking inserts. Monthly range partitioning is the long-term step: billing then reads one partition, and old months can be archived cheaply.

stages.principalRationale: Design the index for the access pattern: billing filters by date for all customers, so the date leads. An index-only scan avoids reading the huge table, CONCURRENTLY keeps it online, and partitioning is the long-term structural fix.

stages.question: How do you ensure this category of problem — query plan regression at production scale — does not recur for future billing queries?

options.label: A
options.text: CI plan tests: EXPLAIN key queries on production-sized data and fail when a big table is fully scanned or a plan changes.
options.feedback: Correct. Automated query plan tests with production-scale data catch regressions before they reach production. The assertion (no Seq Scan on large tables) provides a clear pass/fail gate. Comparing plans between deployments (is the plan worse than before?) detects regressions introduced by schema or data distribution changes. This requires maintaining a production-scale test dataset, which is an infrastructure investment justified by preventing 6-hour billing failures.

options.label: B
options.text: Require EXPLAIN output for every billing query in code review, and block the merge if the plan contains a Seq Scan anywhere.
options.feedback: Manual EXPLAIN review in code review is a step in the right direction but has limitations: reviewers may not have access to production-sized data to test against, Seq Scan on a small table may be correct (not all Seq Scans are problems), and code review is easy to skip under deadline pressure. Automated testing against production-scale data provides stronger guarantees.

options.label: C
options.text: Set statement_timeout to 10 minutes on the billing connection, so a slow query fails quickly instead of running for hours.
options.feedback: Timeouts are a safety valve, not a prevention strategy. A 10-minute timeout would have terminated the billing job after 10 minutes — but the billing still would not have completed. Customers would not have been billed. The goal is to fix the query, not to fail it faster.

options.label: D
options.text: Run ANALYZE on all large tables before every monthly billing run, so the planner always has fresh statistics.
options.feedback: Running ANALYZE before the billing job ensures fresh statistics, which helps the planner make better decisions. But it does not prevent the missing-index problem: even with perfect statistics, the planner cannot use an index that does not exist. Fresh statistics on a table with a full sequential scan means the planner knows exactly how many rows it is scanning — it still must scan them all.

stages.principalRationale: Query plan regression testing against production-scale data is the only reliable way to catch this category of bug before it reaches production. The investment (maintaining a production-scale test dataset) pays for itself after the first prevented incident.

debrief.summary: The billing query used the same plan in staging and production — a full scan of transactions — but production is 200 times larger. An index led by created_at (with the other needed columns included) lets the query read only one month, built online with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Plan regression tests on production-sized data stop this class of problem returning.
keyTakeaways: The same plan can be cheap on small data and catastrophic on large data
Design indexes around the access pattern: here the date range comes first
INCLUDE columns enable index-only scans and avoid reading the table
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY adds indexes to live tables without blocking writes
A WHERE condition on the right table of a LEFT JOIN turns it into an inner join
Test query plans against production-sized data in CI
furtherReading: PostgreSQL documentation — Using EXPLAIN
PostgreSQL documentation — Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes

scenarios.title: The API Breaking Change
scenarios.subtitle: Silent Breaking Change in Payment API Breaks Three Client Integrations
scenarios.context:
The payments API v1 has been live for 18 months. It returns:
```json
{ "status": "SUCCESS", "amount": 100.00, "reference": "PAY-123" }
```
The team deploys a new version that improves the response:
```json
{ "status": "COMPLETED", "amount": "100.00", "currency": "GBP", "reference": "PAY-123" }
```
Changes: (1) `status` value renamed from `SUCCESS` to `COMPLETED`, (2) `amount` type changed from JSON number to JSON string, (3) `currency` field added.

Three days after deployment, three client teams report broken integrations: iOS app crashes on amount parsing (expects double, gets string), Android app shows incorrect payment status (checks for `SUCCESS` string), partner bank integration fails (amount field validation). No internal tests failed pre-deployment.
systemConstraints: API consumed by: iOS app (Swift Codable, strict type mapping), Android app (Kotlin data class), partner bank (OpenAPI schema validation), internal dashboard (JavaScript, flexible parsing)
No API versioning strategy — single endpoint /payments/{id}
No consumer-driven contract tests
Deployment: deployed as a single breaking release, no migration path
Mobile app release cycle: 2-4 weeks for App Store/Play Store approval
Partner bank integration: cannot deploy emergency fix without 48h change window

stages.question: Which of the three changes is a breaking change, and why did internal tests not catch them?

options.label: A
options.text: All three can break a client: the rename breaks string checks, number→string breaks typed parsers, a new field breaks strict schemas. Tests only covered the server side.
options.feedback: Correct. Breaking changes must be evaluated from the consumer's perspective, not the producer's. A change that the server can make freely may break clients with typed deserialisers, exact-value comparisons, or strict schema validation. Internal tests (server-side assertions on the new format) confirm the server works — they cannot detect that clients are expecting the old format. Consumer-driven contract testing exists precisely to close this gap.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the status rename is breaking. A number can always be read as a string, so the amount change is safe, and adding a field is always backward compatible.
options.feedback: All three changes are potentially breaking. Changing amount from JSON number (100.00) to JSON string ('100.00') breaks strictly-typed clients: Swift's Codable cannot map a JSON string to a Double field, and OpenAPI schema validation rejects the wrong type. The status rename breaks exact-string comparisons. Adding a required currency field can break clients that validate the response structure for unexpected fields.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the amount type change is breaking. Renaming an enum value and adding a field are both allowed changes under the OpenAPI specification.
options.feedback: OpenAPI spec allows field additions as backward compatible, but the spec describes the server's output — not the client's parsing behaviour. Clients that check status == 'SUCCESS' in their business logic are broken by the rename regardless of OpenAPI compatibility. The OpenAPI spec does not govern client code — consumer-driven contracts do.

options.label: D
options.text: None of them are breaking: the response is still valid JSON, and well-written clients should parse defensively and ignore anything they do not expect.
options.feedback: Defensive parsing is an aspirational client design principle, not a guarantee. Typed deserialisers in modern mobile languages (Swift, Kotlin, TypeScript) provide type safety precisely by rejecting unexpected types — that is their feature, not a bug. API providers cannot require clients to implement defensive parsing as a prerequisite for backward compatibility. The API contract must be stable.

stages.principalRationale: Breaking changes are determined by what clients actually do with the response, not by what the API spec says is compatible. Consumer-driven contract testing captures the client's actual expectations and fails CI if the provider breaks them — before deployment.

stages.question: What versioning and evolution strategy prevents this class of problem for the payment API?

options.label: A
options.text: Breaking changes only in a new version (/v2); keep /v1 unchanged with a published deprecation period and contract tests; retire it once all consumers moved.
options.feedback: Correct. URL-based versioning is explicit (clients choose their version), easy to route (API gateway or separate handler per version), and allows clients with long release cycles (mobile apps, partner banks) to migrate at their pace. A deprecation window of, for example, 90 days accommodates the mobile app 2–4 week App Store cycle with 2–3 release iterations for migration. Automated contract tests ensuring v1 shape never changes are the enforcement mechanism.

options.label: B
options.text: Version through headers: clients send Accept-Version: 1.x and the server returns the matching format, with X-API-Version on every response.
options.feedback: Header-based versioning works but requires all clients to understand and implement the Accept-Version header — a client that does not send the header gets the latest version and may break. Mobile clients that are deployed and cannot be updated quickly would need to be updated to send the header before the server deploys the new version — still a coordination problem. URL-based versioning (v1/ vs v2/) is more explicit and easier to route.

options.label: C
options.text: Never break anything: only add fields. Keep status=SUCCESS and add statusV2, keep the numeric amount and add amountString next to it.
options.feedback: Additive-only evolution is an admirable constraint but is not always practical. Renaming status values, correcting type mistakes, and removing deprecated fields are legitimate API evolution operations. The 'additive only' rule prevents necessary breaking changes and leads to APIs cluttered with deprecated dual-representation fields. Versioning provides a clean migration path without requiring permanent backward-compat shims.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish an OpenAPI schema and require every consumer to validate their client against it in their own CI, with notice of schema changes before each release.
options.feedback: OpenAPI schema distribution and notification is a useful communication mechanism but relies on consumers proactively updating their tests when the schema changes. Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) inverts this: consumers publish their expectations; the provider CI validates against all consumer expectations before deployment. This is more reliable than notification-based coordination.

stages.principalRationale: URL-based versioning with deprecation windows is the most common and practical API versioning strategy for financial APIs with heterogeneous consumer populations (mobile apps, partner banks, internal services) with different deployment velocities.

stages.question: URL versioning is in place. What testing technique prevents breaking changes from being deployed to any version without being caught in CI?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumer-driven contracts (Pact): each consumer publishes what it really relies on, and the API's CI verifies every contract before deploying.
options.feedback: Correct. Pact inverts the testing relationship: consumers define what they need; the provider verifies it delivers that. When the iOS team adds parsing for amount as Double, their Pact contract records this expectation. When the payment API tries to change amount to String, pact-verify fails CI — the iOS contract is violated. This catches breaking changes before deployment, regardless of which team made the change. Consumer contracts are versioned alongside the consumer code.

options.label: B
options.text: Schema tests in the API's own test suite: validate every response against the expected JSON schema and fail the build if the schema changes.
options.feedback: Provider-side schema tests validate the server's output but only validate what the team writing the server thinks the response should look like. They cannot capture what clients actually do with the response — a schema test might pass for the new COMPLETED status while the Android client still expects SUCCESS. This is the same gap that caused the original incident.

options.label: C
options.text: End-to-end tests that run the real iOS, Android and partner integrations against the API in staging before every deployment.
options.feedback: End-to-end tests with real client apps are valuable for final verification but are slow (require building and deploying all client apps), expensive to maintain, and cannot run mobile apps in CI without a device farm. They also require coordination between teams — mobile apps must have a CI-deployable test build ready. Pact contract tests run as unit tests in each team's CI pipeline, with no coordination required.

options.label: D
options.text: Manual review: an engineering manager approves every API change after comparing the change log with the list of known consumers.
options.feedback: Manual review by a manager is the lowest-leverage control — it relies on human memory of all consumer dependencies, is a bottleneck in the deployment pipeline, and misses implicit dependencies (undocumented internal consumers). Automated contract testing scales to any number of consumers without review bottlenecks.

stages.principalRationale: Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) is the standard solution for this problem. It captures consumer expectations as executable tests, runs them on every provider CI build, and catches breaking changes before deployment — without requiring the provider team to maintain a comprehensive list of all consumers and their expectations.

debrief.summary: API breaking changes are determined by consumer behaviour, not server output. Provider-side tests only validate the server's perspective. Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) captures each consumer's actual expectations and verifies them against every provider deployment. URL-based versioning with deprecation windows allows breaking changes to be introduced safely without requiring simultaneous client updates.
keyTakeaways: Breaking changes: type changes, value renames, field removals — evaluated from consumer parsing perspective
URL versioning (/v1/, /v2/) with 90-day deprecation window is the standard for heterogeneous consumer populations
Pact consumer-driven contracts: consumers publish expectations; provider CI verifies them before deployment
Mobile app release cycles (2-4 weeks) require long deprecation windows — plan accordingly
Adding fields is usually backward-compatible; renaming values and changing types are always breaking
furtherReading: Pact documentation — Consumer-driven contract testing
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann), chapter 4 — Encoding and Evolution

scenarios.title: The Audit Gap
scenarios.subtitle: 5-Year Regulatory Audit Request Reveals 3.5 Years of Missing Records
scenarios.context:
The FCA requests all actions on 47 high-risk customer accounts for a 5-year period. The compliance team runs the extraction. 23 of the 47 accounts have missing records: audit events exist for the last 18 months but nothing before.

Investigation reveals: an archive job was scheduled to move audit records older than 90 days from PostgreSQL to S3. The job was designed as DELETE-then-S3-write (delete from DB first, then write to S3). 18 months ago, an IAM permission change broke the S3 write. The job logged a WARNING (not an ERROR) and continued. Records were deleted from PostgreSQL but never written to S3. No reconciliation check verified the archive. The gap covers 3.5 years of audit data.
systemConstraints: audit_events table: PostgreSQL, 90-day hot retention
Archive target: S3 bucket, 5-year retention policy
Archive job: runs nightly at 01:00, deletes records > 90 days from PostgreSQL, writes to S3
Failure mode: S3 write silently failed (WARNING log) for 18 months
Missing data: 23 accounts × ~3.5 years = estimated 50,000+ missing audit events
Regulatory requirement: FATF Recommendation 11 — 5-year retention of transaction records
On-call alert: none configured for archive job failures

stages.question: What is the root cause of the data loss, and what design principle was violated?

options.label: A
options.text: The IAM change was not tested. Proper change management would have tested S3 write access before the permission change went live, and the archive would not have broken.
options.feedback: Inadequate change management testing contributed to the initial breakage. However, the more fundamental issue is the archive job's design: it deleted records before confirming successful S3 write. Even perfect change management cannot prevent all permission changes from breaking archive jobs over a 5-year period. The design must be resilient to failures — which means write-then-delete, not delete-then-write.

options.label: B
options.text: It deleted from the source before the destination write was confirmed, logged the S3 failure as a warning, and never reconciled counts.
options.feedback: Correct. This is a data durability design failure. The delete-then-write pattern is irreversible: once records are deleted, the source of truth is gone. The correct pattern is write-first: (1) write to S3, (2) verify S3 object count matches source count, (3) only delete from PostgreSQL if verification passes, (4) alert and abort if S3 write fails — never delete. The 'treat S3 failure as WARNING and continue' decision compounded the error by silently destroying data.

options.label: C
options.text: S3 versioning was not enabled. With versioning, the deleted objects would have been kept as older versions behind delete markers and could simply be restored.
options.feedback: S3 bucket versioning would not help here: the objects were never written to S3 in the first place. Versioning only retains overwritten or deleted objects that were previously written. Enabling versioning is a good defence against accidental deletion of S3 objects, but it cannot recover records that never reached S3.

options.label: D
options.text: The audit table was not partitioned. With partitions, old months could have been detached and kept locally instead of deleted, giving a second copy of the data.
options.feedback: Partition detachment (instead of DELETE) is a valid retention strategy for PostgreSQL and would have preserved the data locally. However, it does not address the broader design problem: the archive job had no verification step and treated archive failure as non-fatal. Even with partitioned data, the design principle (write-first, verify, then delete/detach) must be maintained.

stages.principalRationale: Data migration and archiving must be designed with the write-first principle: the destination is confirmed before the source is modified. This principle extends to all data movement operations in financial systems. Treating a data destruction failure as a WARNING rather than a FATAL error is the deeper design failure.

stages.question: Redesign the archive job with correct durability guarantees. What is the correct implementation?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication, so every archive file is copied automatically to a second bucket in another region.
options.feedback: Cross-Region Replication replicates objects that ARE written to S3 — it cannot recover objects that were never written. The problem is the initial S3 write failure, not replication. CRR does not help here.

options.label: B
options.text: Write, verify, then delete: write each batch to S3, read back and count, delete only if it matches, otherwise stop and page. Plus a nightly count check.
options.feedback: Correct. This implements the write-first principle with explicit verification and hard failure on S3 errors. The reconciliation step provides ongoing assurance: even if the job logic has a bug, the nightly reconciliation catches count discrepancies before they accumulate for 18 months. The on-call alert converts a silent failure into a detected incident within 24 hours.

options.label: C
options.text: Stream audit events continuously to an S3 data lake with CDC (Debezium and Kafka Connect), so every record is copied long before the 90-day deletion happens.
options.feedback: CDC-based streaming archival is a robust architecture for financial audit data: it eliminates the batch archive job entirely and provides near-real-time S3 durability. This is better than the batch approach for new data. However, it requires significant infrastructure investment (Debezium + Kafka Connect) and does not solve the existing 50,000+ missing events. It is an architectural improvement, not an immediate remediation.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep all audit data in PostgreSQL for the full 5 years and drop the archive job, using partitioning to keep the table manageable.
options.feedback: Eliminating the archive job removes the failure mode. However, 5 years of audit data in PostgreSQL at current ingestion rates would be a multi-terabyte table requiring significant storage and backup infrastructure investment. S3 is the correct long-term storage for cold audit data. Fixing the archive job design is more cost-effective than retaining 5 years in PostgreSQL.

stages.principalRationale: Write-first + verify + alert is the correct pattern for all data migration jobs that touch regulatory data. The nightly reconciliation is the independent verification layer that catches any bugs in the job logic before they cause unrecoverable data loss.

stages.question: Beyond the archive job fix, what architectural pattern provides the strongest evidence to regulators that the audit trail is complete and has not been tampered with?

options.label: A
options.text: Store a daily checksum of each account's audit records in a separate table, so regulators can check that the records they receive match the stored checksum.
options.feedback: Daily checksums per account provide some integrity assurance but can be faked by an adversary who also modifies the checksum table. The checksum and the data are stored in the same system and subject to the same access controls. A tamper-evident hash chain, where each record depends on all previous records, is significantly harder to falsify — modifying any record requires recalculating all subsequent hashes.

options.label: B
options.text: Use PostgreSQL row-level security so the application role can only INSERT into audit_events — no UPDATE or DELETE permissions at all.
options.feedback: Row-level security preventing modifications is an important access control layer — it raises the bar for insider tampering. However, a superuser (which DBAs typically have) can bypass RLS. For regulatory evidence, cryptographic proof (hash chain) is stronger than access control proof because it can be independently verified without trusting the access control system. Both controls should be used together: RLS prevents casual modification; hash chain detects sophisticated tampering.

options.label: C
options.text: Hash-chain the audit records only: each record stores SHA-256 of its content plus the previous record's hash, and a weekly job recomputes the whole chain.
options.feedback: A strong control for detecting tampering and gaps, but detection alone does not prevent deletion — the archive job in this incident would still have been able to delete records; you would only learn about it later. Pair it with WORM storage so records cannot be removed in the first place.

options.label: D
options.text: Prevention plus proof: WORM storage (S3 Object Lock, compliance mode) and a hash chain that makes any gap or change detectable, verified on a schedule.
options.feedback: Correct. Object Lock in compliance mode prevents anyone — including administrators — from deleting or changing archived records during the retention period. The hash chain (each record stores a hash of its content plus the previous hash) proves the sequence is complete and unchanged, including across the PostgreSQL-to-S3 boundary. Scheduled verification turns this into evidence you can show regulators, not just a design claim.

stages.principalRationale: The strongest regulatory evidence combines prevention and proof. WORM storage (S3 Object Lock in compliance mode) stops anyone deleting or changing records during the retention period; a hash chain gives cryptographic, independently verifiable proof that nothing was removed, changed or inserted. Access controls such as row-level security add a further layer, but on their own they can be bypassed by privileged users.

debrief.summary: Data archiving for regulatory compliance is a financial operations problem, not just an infrastructure task. The write-first principle prevents data loss; hash chaining provides tamper evidence; nightly reconciliation provides ongoing assurance. Any job that deletes regulatory data must treat failure as fatal and alert immediately.
keyTakeaways: Write-first principle: confirm destination write before deleting from source — always, for regulatory data
Archive job failures must be FATAL, not WARNING — data destruction must never proceed silently
Nightly reconciliation: compare source counts against destination counts — catches bugs before 18 months pass
Hash chain: SHA-256(payload + previous_hash) = cryptographic tamper evidence across the full retention period
FATF Recommendation 11: 5-year retention — design for this from day one, not as an afterthought
furtherReading: AWS documentation — S3 Object Lock (compliance mode)
FATF Recommendation 11 — Record keeping

scenarios.title: The Split Brain
scenarios.subtitle: Network Partition in an Active-Active Banking Platform Leaves Transfers Half-Done
scenarios.context:
Active-active banking platform: London (3 CockroachDB nodes) and Frankfurt (3 CockroachDB nodes) in one 6-node cluster. At 14:30, a fibre cut causes a full network partition between the regions. Both regions keep serving their local customers.

At 15:45 the partition heals. End-of-day reconciliation then finds 3 accounts whose cross-region transfers do not balance: for example, £400 left a London customer's account but never arrived in the Frankfurt beneficiary's account. The head of risk asks: 'I thought CockroachDB with Raft consensus was split-brain resistant. How did we lose track of money?'
systemConstraints: CockroachDB, 6 nodes: 3 in London (eu-west-1a/b/c), 3 in Frankfurt (eu-central-1a/b/c)
Account tables: REGIONAL BY ROW — each account row and its voting replicas live in its home region
GLOBAL tables (e.g. payment_transactions) replicate across both regions: writes need a majority of all replicas
Kafka MirrorMaker 2: bidirectional replication of event topics
Cross-region Saga in progress at 14:30: London debit (step 1 committed), Frankfurt credit (step 2 pending)
Partition duration: 75 minutes

stages.question: How did 3 accounts develop conflicting balances despite CockroachDB using Raft consensus?

options.label: A
options.text: A Raft bug: with 6 nodes split 3–3, both halves wrongly believed they had a majority and accepted writes for the same rows independently.
options.feedback: Raft does not allow two majorities. For data replicated across both regions, a 3–3 split leaves neither side with a majority, so those writes simply stop (as they did for the GLOBAL tables). This is not a CockroachDB bug — the cause lies in how the account data is placed and in the half-finished Saga.

options.label: B
options.text: Each region kept a majority for its own REGIONAL BY ROW data. The 3 accounts were mid-Saga: the London debit committed, the Frankfurt credit never ran.
options.feedback: Correct. With REGIONAL BY ROW, an account row's voting replicas live in its home region, so London can keep a majority for London-homed accounts — and Frankfurt for Frankfurt-homed ones — while cut off from each other. That is deliberate: each region stays available for its own customers. Nothing was 'split-brained' in the database. The problem is a Saga that spanned the partition: step 1 (the London debit) committed, and step 2 (the Frankfurt credit) could not run, leaving a debit without a matching credit.

options.label: C
options.text: Bidirectional Kafka replication (MirrorMaker 2) delivered the same payment events in both regions during the partition, so each region credited the same accounts.
options.feedback: Kafka MirrorMaker 2 is used for event replication — it does not directly modify account balances. Account balance updates are done by the application reading Kafka events and writing to CockroachDB. MirrorMaker 2 replication lag during the partition would cause delayed processing of Frankfurt events in London (and vice versa) but not direct balance conflicts. The balance conflict arose from the Saga's partial execution at the partition boundary.

options.label: D
options.text: Account balances were in GLOBAL tables, which serve stale reads; during the partition each region read a different balance and the writes diverged.
options.feedback: GLOBAL tables in CockroachDB give fast, consistent reads in every region at the cost of slower writes; they do not diverge, and during this partition their writes stopped because no majority was available. In any case, the constraints say account balances use REGIONAL BY ROW. The imbalance comes from the half-finished Saga, not from GLOBAL tables.

stages.principalRationale: REGIONAL BY ROW is a deliberate availability choice: each region stays autonomous for its own rows during a partition. Raft still prevents split-brain inside each range, but it cannot make a business workflow that spans two regions atomic. CAP applies to the workflow and data model, not only to the database.

stages.question: After the partition heals, how should the 3 accounts with the incomplete Sagas be resolved?

options.label: A
options.text: Let CockroachDB resolve it automatically with last-write-wins once the partition heals, because it is designed to reconcile conflicting rows.
options.feedback: CockroachDB does not 'resolve conflicts' with last-write-wins — it is serializable, and from its point of view both the committed London debit and the missing Frankfurt credit are perfectly valid states. A debit without a matching credit is a business-level inconsistency the database cannot see. Business logic must decide whether to run the pending credit, reverse the debit, or escalate.

options.label: B
options.text: Find Sagas in progress at partition time: complete the finished ones, resume the missing credits, and reverse the debit plus alert if a credit still fails.
options.feedback: Correct. The Saga event store is the source of truth. Each Saga step is recorded with its outcome — after the partition heals, the Saga orchestrator can query which Sagas were interrupted and determine their resolution path. The key principle: a debit without a credit is a financial emergency that must be automatically compensated or escalated, not left ambiguous. The 3 accounts need explicit resolution, not automatic database conflict resolution.

options.label: C
options.text: Treat London as authoritative: discard Frankfurt's writes from the partition period and replay London's events to Frankfurt.
options.feedback: Discarding Frankfurt writes would destroy legitimate Frankfurt-homed account transactions that occurred during the partition. Frankfurt was autonomously serving its local customers correctly during the partition — those are real transactions. There is no basis for treating London as 'authoritative' and Frankfurt as 'secondary' in an active-active architecture.

options.label: D
options.text: Have the finance team review the 3 accounts by hand, decide the correct balances, and post adjusting entries through the back-office system.
options.feedback: Manual review is a last resort for the most complex cases. For 3 accounts with identifiable Saga state, automated compensation (using the Saga event store) is faster, more consistent, and creates a proper audit trail. Manual adjusting entries require additional approval workflows and may not create the correct double-entry ledger records. Automated Saga compensation is preferred when the Saga state is clear.

stages.principalRationale: The Saga event store is the source of truth for distributed transaction state. Post-partition recovery is a Saga completion problem, not a database conflict resolution problem. Each incomplete Saga must be driven to completion (or compensation) using the recorded event history.

stages.question: What design change prevents Sagas from being left in inconsistent state during future partitions?

options.label: A
options.text: Use synchronous replication for every account operation, so London transactions wait for Frankfurt and nothing is written on either side during a partition.
options.feedback: Synchronous cross-region replication for all account operations would mean a network partition makes both regions unable to serve writes — a complete outage. This trades availability for consistency, which is the opposite of the active-active architecture's design intent. The correct approach is to make Sagas partition-aware, not to eliminate partition tolerance.

options.label: B
options.text: Partition-aware Sagas: park in AWAITING_REGION while the other region is unreachable, resume when it returns, and compensate after an agreed limit.
options.feedback: Correct. Saga partition awareness prevents the partial execution scenario: if the Saga detects that the target region is unreachable before step 2, it parks (does not debit) rather than committing step 1 and failing step 2. The AWAITING_REGION state is an explicit, monitored state — not an ambiguous mid-flight failure. When connectivity restores, the Saga resumes cleanly. The timeout-based compensation provides a bounded SLA for transfers: customers are informed within the SLA window whether their transfer will complete or be compensated.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a third region (e.g. Paris) so a failure between any two regions still leaves a majority available for cross-region data.
options.feedback: A third region increases resilience to 2-node partition scenarios but does not eliminate partition risk. Any 3-node partition that isolates one region still creates the cross-region Saga problem: a Saga step committed in London may fail in Frankfurt if Frankfurt loses its 3 nodes. The fundamental design issue is Sagas spanning partition boundaries — the third region addresses quorum availability but not Saga idempotency across partitions.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace the cross-region Saga with two-phase commit, so the London debit and the Frankfurt credit either both commit or both roll back.
options.feedback: 2PC across regions is a blocking protocol: if Frankfurt is unavailable, the London coordinator holds its locks and waits indefinitely (or until timeout, causing rollback). This creates the 'London transfers are blocked whenever Frankfurt is degraded' problem — worse availability than the Saga pattern. 2PC is not suitable for cross-region financial transactions due to its blocking nature and lock duration.

stages.principalRationale: Saga partition awareness makes the partition a first-class citizen: Sagas can observe and respond to regional unavailability rather than failing mid-flight. The AWAITING_REGION state is an explicit, bounded, monitored state that can be retried on recovery or compensated on timeout. This is the correct pattern for multi-region financial workflows.

debrief.summary: Active-active multi-region architectures trade global consistency for availability during partitions. REGIONAL BY ROW data models make each region autonomous — which is the feature, not a bug. The design challenge is Sagas that span regions: they must be partition-aware, parking in a safe state when the target region is unreachable, rather than committing step 1 and failing step 2. The Saga event store is the source of truth for post-partition recovery.
keyTakeaways: REGIONAL BY ROW: each region is autonomous for its home rows — intentional AP design for account reads
Raft never allows two majorities; REGIONAL BY ROW simply places each row's majority in its home region
Cross-region Sagas are the highest-risk pattern — they span the partition boundary and can partially commit
Saga partition awareness: check regional connectivity before step 1, park in AWAITING_REGION if unreachable
Post-partition recovery: query Saga event store, complete or compensate each interrupted Saga
furtherReading: CockroachDB documentation — Multi-region: REGIONAL BY ROW tables and survival goals
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann), chapter 9 — Consistency and Consensus

scenarios.title: The Microservice Maze
scenarios.subtitle: Decomposing a 99.95% Availability Monolith into 15 Microservices
scenarios.context:
The engineering VP proposes decomposing the payment monolith into 15 microservices — one per squad (8 squads). The stated motivation: 'teams are blocking each other on deployments.' The monolith currently: processes 25,000 TPS, has 99.95% availability (4.38 hours/month error budget), deploys twice per week.

You are the Principal Engineer. The VP wants a decision within 2 weeks. The timeline is 6 months. Each squad would own their service end-to-end (codebase, database, deployments). You must assess the proposal and recommend a path forward.
systemConstraints: Monolith: Java 21, Spring Boot, single PostgreSQL, 25,000 TPS, 99.95% availability
Team structure: 8 squads × 4 engineers = 32 engineers
Deployment coupling cause: shared database schema, all tests must pass before any squad deploys

Planned services: Payment Initiation, Authorisation, Fraud, Routing, FX, Settlement, Ledger, Notification, Account, Limits, Compliance, Reporting, Reference Data, Auth/Identity, API Gateway (15 services)
Current deployment pipeline: 45 minutes, deploys entire monolith
Financial operations: account debit + balance check + fraud check + ledger entry = single ACID transaction today

stages.question: What is the primary architectural risk of decomposing the payment flow into 15 microservices within 6 months?

options.label: A
options.text: Cost: infrastructure grows with the number of services. 15 services, each with its own pods and database, will cost about 10× the current monolith.
options.feedback: Infrastructure cost increases are real but manageable — services can share infrastructure components. This is an operational concern, not an architectural risk. The VP can be convinced to fund the infrastructure. The architectural risks (consistency, availability, complexity) are more fundamental and harder to reverse once the decomposition is complete.

options.label: B
options.text: A single ACID transaction becomes a distributed one, and 15 chained services at 99.95% give ~99.25%. Deployment coupling can be fixed without a network.
options.feedback: Correct on all three dimensions. (1) ACID → Saga: the monolith's atomic financial operations become eventually consistent distributed workflows — a fundamental correctness trade-off. (2) The availability multiplication law: each service's availability compounds, making the system worse overall unless each service significantly exceeds the target. (3) The root cause (deployment coupling) is likely a code organisation problem, not a network boundary problem — it can be fixed without microservices. Solving a deployment coupling problem with distributed systems introduces much larger problems.

options.label: C
options.text: Skills: the teams would need to learn Kubernetes, a service mesh and distributed tracing, a gap too large to close in 6 months.
options.feedback: Skill gaps are real and important to address in the timeline. However, skill gaps are solvable with training and hiring. The architectural consequences (distributed transactions, reduced availability, operational complexity) persist after engineers become proficient. The architectural risks are the harder constraints.

options.label: D
options.text: Complexity: 15 services calling each other over HTTP create a fragile dependency graph that depends heavily on service discovery and load balancing.
options.feedback: Operational complexity of service mesh is a real concern but is a solvable problem with Kubernetes, Istio, and observability tooling. The more fundamental risks are the ACID → eventual consistency trade-off and the aggregate availability math. These are architectural properties that cannot be tooled away.

stages.principalRationale: The availability multiplication law is a mathematical consequence of microservice decomposition that many teams discover too late. For a payment platform targeting 99.95%, each service must achieve much higher individual availability to maintain the aggregate. The ACID → Saga trade-off is an even more fundamental correctness regression for financial operations.

stages.question: What is the most effective path forward that solves the actual problem (deployment coupling) without the microservice architectural risks?

options.label: A
options.text: Go ahead with 15 services but hire 3 senior distributed-systems engineers to manage the extra complexity, since the VP has already committed to the direction.
options.feedback: Proceeding with a flawed architecture because a VP committed to it is a failure of principal engineering judgment. The VP hired a Principal Engineer precisely to surface architectural risks before they become production incidents. Recommending proceeding with known risks without raising them is a dereliction of the role.

options.label: B
options.text: Split into 4 coarse services (Payments Core, Compliance, Reporting, Customer) instead of 15, which gives squads some autonomy with fewer distributed transactions.
options.feedback: 4 coarse-grained services is better than 15 fine-grained ones — it reduces the number of Saga boundaries and the aggregate availability degradation. However, the financial core (Payments Core) would still need to span multiple squad domains (Authorisation, Fraud, Ledger are all in 'Payments Core'). Deployment coupling within the Payments Core service would persist. The modular monolith approach solves deployment coupling more precisely — without network boundaries — while preserving ACID properties.

options.label: C
options.text: Modular monolith: enforced module boundaries and separate pipelines per squad; extract only 2–3 non-financial services and keep the money core together.
options.feedback: Correct. This solves the stated problem (deployment coupling) through module isolation and separate test pipelines, without introducing distributed transaction risk to the financial core. Extracting non-financial services first (services that do not participate in ACID transactions) allows the team to build distributed systems competence at low risk. The strangler-fig pattern applied selectively — not big-bang decomposition. The VP's deployment velocity goal is achieved; the financial integrity risk is managed.

options.label: D
options.text: Introduce event sourcing and CQRS inside the monolith, so each squad owns event handlers and read models fed from one shared event log.
options.feedback: Event sourcing + CQRS within a monolith is a valid architectural pattern for domain separation. It addresses read-side coupling effectively but does not address the write-side deployment coupling: all squads still share the same event store and must coordinate schema changes. It also adds significant complexity without directly solving the stated problem (deployment blocking on shared test suite).

stages.principalRationale: Principal Engineers must distinguish the stated problem (deployment coupling) from the proposed solution (microservices). Module isolation and separate pipelines solve deployment coupling without distributed system complexity. Selective extraction of non-financial services builds competence at low risk. The financial core stays monolithic until the team earns the right to distribute it.

stages.question: If the company decides to proceed with partial microservice extraction anyway, what is the success metric that proves the extraction was worth the complexity cost?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of services running in production — every extracted service is measurable progress towards the target architecture.
options.feedback: Number of services is a vanity metric. Each additional service adds complexity and availability risk. A team that has deployed 15 services but has 97% aggregate availability and 3× more deployment incidents than the monolith has made negative progress, regardless of service count.

options.label: B
options.text: Lead time for changes: the time from commit to production, which directly measures whether teams can ship faster.
options.feedback: Lead time is an important metric but tells only one part of the story. A microservice with 10-minute lead time that causes 3 incidents per week is worse than a monolith with 45-minute lead time and 0 incidents per week. Lead time must be tracked alongside change failure rate and availability to be meaningful.

options.label: C
options.text: Deployment frequency per squad, change failure rate and availability against the SLO — all three together.
options.feedback: Correct. These three DORA-adjacent metrics directly measure whether the decomposition achieved its goal (deployment independence) without regressing on its constraints (reliability). Deployment frequency proves squads can deploy independently. Change failure rate proves deployments are safer (or at least no worse). Aggregate availability proves the system is as reliable as the monolith. If any of the three regresses, the decomposition has not succeeded — regardless of how many services are running.

options.label: D
options.text: Engineer satisfaction surveys: if engineers enjoy working in the new architecture more, the decomposition has paid off.
options.feedback: Engineer satisfaction is a valid input (unhappy engineers leave, reducing team stability) but cannot be the success criterion for an architectural decision with financial and regulatory implications. A team that enjoys microservices but runs at 98.5% availability has failed on the fundamental SLO constraint. Business and reliability outcomes must take precedence.

stages.principalRationale: DORA metrics (deployment frequency, change failure rate, lead time, MTTR) provide evidence-based measurement of DevOps performance. For microservice extraction, success requires improvement across all three dimensions simultaneously: velocity, reliability, and availability. Any metric-gaming (e.g., deploy more frequently by deploying broken code) is visible across the full set.

debrief.summary: Microservice decomposition is a trade-off, not an upgrade. The benefits (team autonomy, independent deployment) come at the cost of distributed transaction complexity, reduced aggregate availability, and operational overhead. The correct principal engineering judgment is to solve the stated problem (deployment coupling) with the minimum necessary complexity — often module isolation within the monolith — rather than immediately introducing network boundaries.
keyTakeaways: Availability multiplication: N services at 99.95% → (0.9995)^N aggregate. At N=15: 99.25%. This is worse than the monolith.
ACID → Saga: decomposing financial operations across service boundaries replaces transactions with eventual consistency
Deployment coupling is usually a code organisation problem, not a network boundary problem
Modular monolith + ArchUnit enforced boundaries solves deployment coupling without distributed system risk
Extract non-financial services first (Notifications, Reference Data) to build distributed systems competence at low risk
Success metrics: deployment frequency + change failure rate + aggregate availability — all three must improve
furtherReading: Sam Newman — Monolith to Microservices
Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble & Gene Kim — Accelerate (DORA metrics)
